findings.claim: DRCT trains the detector with diffusion reconstructions of real images in the FAKE class. Four sample types are used (real, real reconstructed, fake, fake reconstructed) and only the untouched real image is 'real'. The reconstructed real images are called hard samples that keep the content but carry the generator fingerprint.
findings.source: Chen, Zeng, Yang, Yang. DRCT: Diffusion Reconstruction Contrastive Training towards Universal Detection of Diffusion Generated Images. ICML 2024, PMLR 235:7621-7639. https://proceedings.mlr.press/v235/chen24ay.html (PDF text read)
findings.quote: The two loss functions guide the classifier to learn a better feature representation and to identify real images as real and the other three types of images as fake.
findings.bears_on: Q1. In generated-image detection a one-image reconstruction is labelled fake. This supports the author's view only in the sense that flagging a reconstruction is the generated-image detection task by that field's own definition; it does not say the image is bona fide for a morph detector.

findings.claim: Aligned Datasets builds its whole fake class by passing real images once through the latent diffusion autoencoder (encode, decode, no denoising). The authors say the outputs are near identical to the real images and are fake only because they carry generator artifacts.
findings.source: Rajan, Usman, Sud, Lee et al. Aligned Datasets Improve Detection of Latent Diffusion-Generated Images. arXiv:2410.11835 (HTML read). ICLR 2025 per an ICLR proceedings URL seen in search results; proceedings page not opened.
findings.quote: These reconstructions are near-identical to their real counterparts visually- e.g., in resolution, semantic content and color tone, except that they have artifacts introduced through the generative model. Hence, they serve as our fake images.
findings.bears_on: Q1. Clear statement that a VAE reconstruction of one real photo is 'fake' in generated-image detection. Label is defined by the process trace, not by content or intent.

findings.claim: B-Free builds fakes as 'self-conditioned reconstructions' of real COCO images (Stable Diffusion 2.1 inpainting pipeline) plus inpainted variants, including a variant where the original real background is pasted back. All of these go in the fake class; the paper does not discuss whether a content-preserving regeneration should count as real.
findings.source: Guillaro, Zingarini, Usman, Sud, Cozzolino, Verdoliva. A Bias-Free Training Paradigm for More General AI-generated Image Detection. CVPR 2025, pp. 18685-18694 (CVF page opened); arXiv:2412.17671 (HTML read).
findings.quote: To avoid possible biases, we generate synthetic images from self-conditioned reconstructions of real images and include augmentation in the form of inpainted versions.
findings.bears_on: Q1. Same labelling as DRCT and Aligned Datasets: reconstruction of a real image is fake, and a locally edited real image is fake too.

findings.claim: Dual Data Alignment uses VAE reconstructions of real images as the synthetic class in training and in its DDA-COCO test set (listed as 5K real and 25K fake). It reports that a frequency detector flags visually identical reconstructions 93% of the time and treats that as evidence of a frequency shortcut, not as evidence that the label is wrong.
findings.source: Chen et al. Dual Data Alignment Makes AI-Generated Image Detector Easier Generalizable. arXiv:2505.14359 (HTML read); arXiv comment says 'NeurIPS 2025 Spotlight'.
findings.quote: visually identical VAE-reconstructed images are detected by the frequency-based detector SAFE [ 23 ] with a 93% success rate, indicating a significant difference in the frequency domain.
findings.bears_on: Q1. Reconstruction is fake by construction. Also a warning relevant to the paper: reconstructions differ from camera images in frequency content, so a detector can separate them without using any morph cue.

findings.claim: The reconstruction-as-fake convention is old and was first used on faces. Chai et al. add GAN inversions ('reprojections') of real CelebA-HQ faces to the fake training set. Zhang, Karaman and Chang (AutoGAN) pass a real image through a GAN-like generator and train on real versus reconstructed.
findings.source: Chai, Bau, Lim, Isola. What makes fake images detectable? Understanding properties that generalize. arXiv:2008.10588 (ar5iv read; ECCV 2020 venue not verified). Zhang, Karaman, Chang. Detecting and Simulating Artifacts in GAN Fake Images. arXiv:1907.06515 (ar5iv read; WIFS 2019 venue not verified).
findings.quote: Intuitively, this reprojection step creates fake images generated by the GAN that are as close as possible to their corresponding real images, forcing the classifier to focus on the remaining differences
findings.bears_on: Q1. Exactly the GAN-inversion case in the question: one real face inverted and re-rendered is treated as fake in synthetic-image detection.

findings.claim: The standard GAN-detection benchmark ForenSynths counts outputs of image-to-image CNNs applied to real captures as 'fake': its eleven fake sources include a super-resolution network (SAN) and Seeing-in-the-Dark low-light enhancement, next to StyleGAN and face-swap deepfakes.
findings.source: Wang, Wang, Zhang, Owens, Efros. CNN-generated images are surprisingly easy to spot... for now. arXiv:1912.11035 (ar5iv read; arXiv comment 'Accepted to CVPR 2020').
findings.quote: We also use a state-of-the-art super-resolution model, the Second Order Attention Network (SAN)
findings.bears_on: Q1 (AI-enhanced images). In this field a neural enhancement of a real photo is in the fake class. The class is 'passed through a CNN generator', which is wider than 'non-existent content'.

findings.claim: DIRE and AEROBLADE use reconstruction only as a measuring tool and are silent on the label of a real image that has itself been reconstructed. DIRE's premise is that generated images reconstruct well and real ones do not. AEROBLADE states that accurate reconstruction of fine detail suggests LDM origin, and calls a real image with an inpainted patch an 'authentic image' with inpainted regions. AEROBLADE also reports that DIRE's published results were affected by a JPEG versus PNG storage bias.
findings.source: Wang et al. DIRE for Diffusion-Generated Image Detection. ICCV 2023, pp. 22445-22455 (CVF page opened); arXiv:2303.09295 (ar5iv read). Ricker, Lukovnikov, Fischer. AEROBLADE. arXiv:2401.17879 (HTML read; arXiv comment 'Accepted to CVPR 2024').
findings.quote: We observe that diffusion-generated images can be approximately reconstructed by a diffusion model while real images cannot.
findings.bears_on: Q1. Silence on the label. By their logic a laundered real photo would score as generated (it reconstructs well), but neither paper says so or discusses it.

findings.claim: Fake or JPEG is about dataset bias (JPEG compression and image size in GenImage), not about reconstructions. It shows detectors learn format differences between the classes. It does not discuss reconstructed or edited real images.
findings.source: Grommelt, Weiss, Pfreundt, Keuper. Fake or JPEG? Revealing Common Biases in Generated Image Detection Datasets. arXiv:2403.17608 (HTML read; venue not verified, our notes say ECCVW 2024).
findings.quote: In this paper, we emphasize that many datasets for AI-generated image detection contain biases related to JPEG compression and image size.
findings.bears_on: Q1, indirectly. Silent on the label question. Relevant as method precedent: processing differences between classes are a confound, which is the argument for pipeline-matched genuine images.

findings.claim: The one paper found that debates the label directly: Mandelli, Bestagini and Tubaro call an SD encode-decode copy of a real photo 'laundering'. They say the copy is in principle synthetic, but treat its classification as plain 'synthetic' as a harmful error because real content gets dismissed, and they propose three classes (pristine, laundered, fully synthetic) with a two-stage detector.
findings.source: Mandelli, Bestagini, Tubaro. When Synthetic Traces Hide Real Content: Analysis of Stable Diffusion Image Laundering. arXiv:2407.10736 (abstract and HTML read; venue not verified).
findings.quote: However, in principle, laundered images are synthetic and not real photographs.
findings.bears_on: Q1. Shows the binary label is contested. Their answer is neither 'real' nor 'fake' but a separate class, which matches the author's idea that a one-photo reconstruction should not be merged into the attack class without comment.

findings.claim: Two forensic papers take the opposite label: a real image passed through a learned autoencoder stays in the real (pristine) class and a 'synthetic' verdict on it is an error. Cozzolino et al. pass real RAISE images through the SDXL autoencoder and call it an attack that adds synthetic traces to real images. Cannas et al. show detectors flag JPEG AI (neural codec) compressed pristine images as synthetic and count these as false alarms.
findings.source: Cozzolino, Poggi, Corvi, Niessner, Verdoliva. Raising the Bar of AI-generated Image Detection with CLIP. arXiv:2312.00195 (ar5iv read; cited by Mandelli et al. as CVPR 2024 proceedings pp. 4356-4366, likely the workshops volume, not verified). Cannas, Mandelli et al. Is JPEG AI going to change image forensics? arXiv:2412.03261 (abstract and HTML read; venue not verified).
findings.quote: attacks can be carried out with the very aim of making everything appear as synthetic, misleading current forensic detectors based on low-level traces, and undermining public trust in forensic analyses.
findings.bears_on: Q1. Supports the author's lean inside the neighbouring field itself: here flagging an autoencoded real image is a false alarm. Second exact quote (Cannas et al.): 'pristine images compressed with this new standard can be mistaken for deepfakes'. So the field has both labels in print, often from overlapping author groups.

findings.claim: Stay-Positive gives an explicit normative definition of the fake class by generator trace: an image is fake if and only if it carries generative-model artifacts. Under this rule any reconstruction is fake regardless of content. The paper reports that detectors built this way are better at catching inpainted real images.
findings.source: Rajan, Lee. Stay-Positive: A Case for Ignoring Real Image Features in Fake Image Detection. arXiv:2502.07778 (abstract read; venue not verified).
findings.quote: We argue that an image should be classified as fake if and only if it contains artifacts introduced by the generative model.
findings.bears_on: Q1. The clearest statement of what generated-image detection is asked to detect: the render trace. That is a different question from 'does this image blend two identities', which is the basis for keeping the two tasks apart.

findings.claim: A 2026 paper shows that AI-image detectors mostly detect the VAE round trip itself and not the synthesized content. Restoring the original pixels outside an inpainted region (keeping all synthesized content) drops detectors toward chance, including the bias-aware DDA (97.6% to 58.4%). The authors attribute 97% of the background spectral shift to the autoencoder round trip alone.
findings.source: Nebioglu, Bilgic, Popescu. AI-Generated Image Detectors Exploit Global Artifacts: Evidence from Inpainting Exchange. arXiv:2602.00192 (abstract and HTML read; arXiv comment 'Accepted to WACV 2027').
findings.quote: state-of-the-art AI-generated image detectors largely fail to identify what was synthesized and instead exploit a global artifact introduced as a side effect of the generation pipeline
findings.bears_on: Q1. Direct evidence that 'reconstruction detected as fake' is a pipeline cue. A morph detector that fires on one-photo reconstructions is most likely using this same cue, which is not morph evidence.

findings.claim: For locally AI-edited real images the field has no single rule. Deepfake-Eval-2024 labels the whole item fake if any portion is AI, while non-AI photoshopped images count as real unless there is evidence of AI. SIDA uses three types (real, fully synthetic, tampered). TGIF separates spliced from fully regenerated inpainting and notes synthetic-image detectors flag the regenerated kind. Semi-Truths grades AI-augmented images by magnitude of change.
findings.source: Chandra et al. Deepfake-Eval-2024. arXiv:2503.02857 (HTML read, labeling codebook B.1). Huang et al. SIDA. arXiv:2412.04292 (abstract and HTML read; CVPR 2025 not verified). Mareen et al. TGIF. arXiv:2407.11566 (abstract read; arXiv comment 'accepted at IEEE WIFS 2024'). Pal et al. Semi-Truths. arXiv:2411.07472 (abstract and HTML read; arXiv comment 'Accepted at NeurIPS 2024 Track Datasets & Benchmarks Track').
findings.quote: If any portion is AI, then entire item is fake
findings.bears_on: Q1 (AI-enhanced and edited photos). Labels are set by each benchmark's purpose. The strictest rule ('any AI makes it fake') is a provenance rule for misinformation work, not a biometric attack definition.

findings.claim: Provenance standards and regulation keep reconstructed or enhanced real media apart from fully generated media. The IPTC Digital Source Type vocabulary has separate codes for 'Created using Generative AI', 'Edited using Generative AI' and 'Algorithmically-altered media'. EU AI Act Article 50(2) exempts from the AI-marking duty systems that only assist standard editing or do not substantially alter the input.
findings.source: IPTC NewsCodes Digital Source Type, https://cv.iptc.org/newscodes/digitalsourcetype/ (opened). EU AI Act Article 50, text as mirrored at https://artificialintelligenceact.eu/article/50/ (opened; unofficial mirror of Regulation (EU) 2024/1689).
findings.quote: Modification or correction by algorithm without changing the main content of the media, initiated or configured by a human, such as sharpening or applying noise reduction
findings.bears_on: Q1. Outside academia the answer is graded, not binary, and a content-preserving algorithmic pass is not classed as 'generated'. AI Act exact text: 'This obligation shall not apply to the extent the AI systems perform an assistive function for standard editing or do not substantially alter the input data'.

findings.claim: A deployed platform ran into this exact label problem. Meta labelled real photos with minor AI retouching as 'Made with AI', withdrew that wording in July 2024, and from September 2024 handles AI-edited content differently from AI-generated content.
findings.source: Meta Newsroom. Our Approach to Labeling AI-Generated Content and Manipulated Media (April 5, 2024, with updates of July 1 and September 2024). https://about.fb.com/news/2024/04/metas-approach-to-labeling-ai-generated-content-and-manipulated-media/ (opened)
findings.quote: For example, some content that included minor modifications using AI, such as retouching tools, included industry standard indicators that were then labeled “Made with AI.”
findings.bears_on: Q1 (AI-enhanced photos). Practical evidence that treating an AI-touched genuine photo as 'generated' is seen as a labelling error by users. Not an academic source.

findings.claim: Tolosana et al. (2020) define four main face manipulation types: entire face synthesis, identity swap, attribute manipulation, expression swap. Face morphing is discussed apart, under 'other' manipulations, and is said to be a different type. Morphing is defined by its biometric purpose: a sample that resembles two or more individuals.
findings.source: Tolosana, Vera-Rodriguez, Fierrez, Morales, Ortega-Garcia. DeepFakes and Beyond: A Survey of Face Manipulation and Fake Detection. arXiv:2001.00179 (ar5iv read; journal Information Fusion 2020 from memory, not verified).
findings.quote: In this sense, face morphing is a different type of facial manipulation compared with the four main types covered in this survey.
findings.bears_on: Q1: supports separating morph detection from entire-face-synthesis detection. Q2: the definition ('Face morphing is a type of face manipulation that can be used to create artificial biometric face samples that resemble the biometric information of two or more individuals') is purpose based and says nothing about same-person or one-image morphs.

findings.claim: The 2022 Handbook lists six manipulation types with face morphing as its own type next to entire face synthesis, and organises detection in separate chapters: ch. 9 'Detection of AI-Generated Synthetic Faces', ch. 15 'Face Morphing Attack Detection Methods', ch. 17 'Facial Retouching and Alteration Detection'. Its closing chapter says detectors drop sharply across manipulation types.
findings.source: Rathgeb, Tolosana, Vera-Rodriguez, Busch (eds.). Handbook of Digital Face Manipulation and Detection. Springer 2022, open access. Read from the OAPEN PDF https://library.oapen.org/bitstream/20.500.12657/52835/1/978-3-030-87664-7.pdf (ch. 1 by Tolosana et al., contents pages, ch. 21). Springer chapter pages could not be opened.
findings.quote: six types of digital face manipulations: (i) entire face synthesis, (ii) identity swap, (iii) face morphing, (iv) attribute manipulation, (v) expression swap (a.k.a. face reenactment or talking faces), and (vi) audio- and text-to-video.
findings.bears_on: Q1: the reference taxonomy treats synthetic-face detection and morph detection as different detection topics. Entire face synthesis is defined as 'This manipulation creates entire non-existent face images', which a one-photo reconstruction of a real person does not match. Q2: the morphing definition again says 'two or more individuals' and is silent on same-person input.

findings.claim: On retouching and beautification the Handbook treats them as a manipulation type with its own detectors, but describes them as usually done by bona fide users without malicious intent and with little security impact. In the chapter 2 experiment, retouched images are a separate scenario ('Retouching mated') from 'Bona fide mated'.
findings.source: Ibsen, Rathgeb, Fischer, Drozdowski, Busch. Digital Face Manipulation in Biometric Systems (Handbook ch. 2). Majumdar, Agarwal, Vatsa, Singh. Facial Retouching and Alteration Detection (Handbook ch. 17). Same OAPEN PDF, read.
findings.quote: other manipulations usually carried out by bona fide users like slight retouching has little to no security implications
findings.bears_on: Q1 (beautified or AI-enhanced photos). The biometrics reference text does not put retouched genuine images in the morph attack class. It keeps them as a third group: manipulated, by a bona fide user. Ch. 17 exact text: 'Retouching is done for beautification purposes, generally, without any malicious intent and can be categorized as unintentional adversary.'

findings.claim: Colbois and Marcel (BIOSIG 2022) asked how close GAN-morph detection is to GAN-image detection. A ResNet pretrained for GAN image detection, used out of the box, was the best system and reached close to perfect accuracy on StyleGAN2 and MIPGAN morphs. Landmark morphs were excluded, with the remark that two independent detectors could be used. A pattern search of the text found no control with GAN-reconstructed bona fide images.
findings.source: Colbois, Marcel. On the detection of morphing attacks generated by GANs. arXiv:2209.00404 (ar5iv read; arXiv comment 'Accepted for publication at BIOSIG 2022').
findings.quote: we establish an overview of deep-MAD capability, in particular evaluating how much the problem is similar to the one of GAN-image detection.
findings.bears_on: Q1. Shows that when bona fide images are camera photos, deep-morph detection can be solved as generated-image detection. It therefore cannot tell 'detects morphing' from 'detects the GAN'. This is the confusion the author wants to avoid; the paper does not resolve it.

findings.claim: Colbois and Marcel (IJCB 2024) explicitly propose to treat MAD as a deepfake or synthetic-image detection problem for deep morphs, while noting that landmark morphs are of a fundamentally different nature and that print-scan is not handled in deepfake work.
findings.source: Colbois, Marcel. Evaluating the Effectiveness of Attack-Agnostic Features for Morphing Attack Detection. IJCB 2024 per Idiap record; PDF read at https://publications.idiap.ch/attachments/papers/2024/Colbois_IJCB2024_2024.pdf
findings.quote: We propose to consider the reverse perspective: treating MAD as a deepfake detection problem, specifically focusing on detecting deep synthetic images.
findings.bears_on: Q1, against the author's lean. A published position that merges the two tasks for GAN and diffusion morphs. The paper should cite it as the opposing view. Under this framing a one-photo reconstruction would be flagged, and the paper does not say whether that counts as an error.

findings.claim: One MAD paper separates the two tasks explicitly and labels GAN reconstructions of genuine images as bona fide: Zhang, Ramachandra, Raja and Busch add reconstructed bona fide images to their GAN-morph datasets so the detector learns morphing patterns, not GAN patterns.
findings.source: Zhang, Ramachandra, Raja, Busch. Generalized Single-Image-Based Morphing Attack Detection Using Deep Representations from Vision Transformer. arXiv:2501.09817 (abstract and HTML read; venue not verified, our notes say CVPRW 2024).
findings.quote: As our target is to train the model to learn patterns generated from morphing instead of general patterns from GANs, reconstructed bona fide images are applied to the datasets with GAN-based morphing algorithms.
findings.bears_on: Q1, in favour of the author's lean, from inside MAD. It is a dataset design choice stated in one sentence, with no argument about class definition and no report of detector error on those images. It is precedent, not a field-wide stand.

findings.claim: SMDD uses fully synthetic single-identity StyleGAN2-ADA faces as the bona fide class and morphs of those faces as attacks (30,000 attack and 50,000 bona fide samples). Pattern searches of the paper found no discussion of whether a synthetic face is bona fide in principle; the motivation given is privacy and law.
findings.source: Damer, Lopez, Fang, Spiller, Pham, Boutros. Privacy-friendly Synthetic Data for the Development of Face Morphing Attack Detectors. arXiv:2203.06691 (ar5iv read; arXiv comment 'Accepted at CVPR Workshops 2022').
findings.quote: The SMDD dataset, consisting of 30,000 attack and 50,000 bona fide samples, is publicly available for research purposes
findings.bears_on: Q1. The MAD community already labels generated one-identity faces as bona fide in a widely used training set, which is the opposite of the generated-image detection label. Done by practice, without a stated definition.

findings.claim: Unified face attack benchmarks that merge physical spoofs with digital forgeries (face swap, attribute edit, entire synthesis, video driven) do not include morphing attacks. In both papers the string 'morph' occurs only in '3D Morphable Model'. No benchmark was found that scores one detector on both morph detection and synthetic-face detection.
findings.source: Fang et al. Unified Physical-Digital Face Attack Detection (UniAttackData). arXiv:2401.17699 (HTML searched; IJCAI 2024 per search result, not verified). Liu et al. Benchmarking Unified Face Attack Detection via Hierarchical Prompt Tuning. arXiv:2505.13327v3 (HTML searched).
findings.bears_on: Q1. The 'unified' face-security literature leaves morphing out, so there is no shared label convention between morph detection and synthetic-face detection to appeal to. Evidence of separation by omission, not by argument.

findings.claim: The DiFF face-forgery benchmark counts single-identity image-conditioned diffusion outputs as forgeries: its Image-to-Image subset is defined as methods that replicate one identity from a visual prompt, next to text-to-image, face swapping and face editing.
findings.source: Cheng, Guo, Wang, Nie, Kankanhalli. Diffusion Facial Forgery Detection. arXiv:2401.15859 (abstract and HTML read; venue not verified).
findings.quote: Specifically, I2I, as illustrated in Figure 5 b , pertains to methods that replicate a single identity.
findings.bears_on: Q1. In face deepfake detection, a diffusion re-render of one real person's face is in the forgery class. Same convention as general generated-image detection, now on faces.

findings.claim: Self-blending is the neighbouring-field precedent closest to Q2. SBI blends one pristine face with a transformed copy of itself and uses the result as a fake training sample. SelfMAD (FG 2025) carries the idea to MAD, simulating morph artifacts from bona fide images. In SelfMAD's comparison table the deepfake method SBI is much weaker on morphs (FRGC-M EER 16.68, 15.32, 52.90 versus SelfMAD 5.59, 2.59, 15.84 for FaceMorpher, OpenCV, StyleGAN2).
findings.source: Shiohara, Yamasaki. Detecting Deepfakes with Self-Blended Images. arXiv:2204.08376 (abstract and ar5iv read; CVPR 2022 as cited in SelfMAD's reference list). Ivanovska et al. SelfMAD. arXiv:2504.05504 (HTML read; arXiv comment 'Accepted at ... FG 2025').
findings.quote: SBIs are generated by blending pseudo source and target images from single pristine images, reproducing common forgery artifacts (e.g., blending boundaries and statistical inconsistencies between source and target images).
findings.bears_on: Q2, partly in favour of the author's lean: a one-image self-blend is labelled by the process (fake or pseudo-morph), not by the number of identities. Limits: these are training surrogates, never an evaluation class, and neither paper argues that such an image is an attack in the operational sense. Also Q1: the SBI numbers show deepfake detectors do not transfer directly to morphs.

stance_summary:
Scope: neighbouring fields only (AI-generated image detection, deepfake detection, face manipulation taxonomies, provenance standards). ISO, NIST and the core MAD literature were not searched here.

Q1, one-photo reconstructions. The neighbouring field has a working convention but no agreed definition, and the convention is inconsistent.
(a) Majority practice in generated-image detection: a real image passed through a generator is FAKE. This goes back to AutoGAN (2019) and Chai et al. (2020, GAN inversion of real faces) and is the basis of DRCT, Aligned Datasets, B-Free and Dual Data Alignment. Stay-Positive states the rule outright: fake if and only if generator artifacts are present. ForenSynths even puts super-resolution and low-light enhancement outputs in the fake class, and DiFF puts single-identity diffusion re-renders of faces in the forgery class. The label is defined by the processing trace, never by content, identity or intent.
(b) Minority but explicit opposite framing, often from the same research groups: Cozzolino et al. call passing a real image through the SDXL autoencoder an attack that makes real content look synthetic, and Cannas et al. count neural-codec (JPEG AI) images flagged as synthetic as false alarms. Here the autoencoded real image stays 'pristine'.
(c) Third-class answers: Mandelli et al. (image laundering) is the only paper found that debates the label. It says the copy is 'in principle' synthetic but proposes three classes: pristine, laundered, fully synthetic. SIDA uses real, fully synthetic, tampered. The IPTC vocabulary, EU AI Act Article 50(2) and Meta's labelling policy all separate content-preserving algorithmic processing or editing from generation.
(d) DIRE, AEROBLADE and Fake or JPEG are silent on the label. The 2026 Inpainting Exchange paper shows detectors key on the VAE round trip and not on what was synthesized, which means 'fires on a reconstruction' is a pipeline cue.
So the literature supports the author's separation of tasks in this sense: generated-image detection defines its positive class as 'carries a generator trace', which is a different question from 'blends two identities'. The face manipulation taxonomies agree: Tolosana et al. say morphing 'is a different type of facial manipulation' from entire face synthesis, and the 2022 Handbook lists them as separate types with separate detection chapters, defining entire face synthesis as creating 'non-existent' faces (a one-photo reconstruction of a real person does not fit). The Handbook also treats retouching as a manipulation typically done by bona fide users. On the MAD side, SMDD uses fully generated one-identity faces as bona fide, and Zhang et al. (arXiv 2501.09817) add GAN-reconstructed bona fide images 'to learn patterns generated from morphing instead of general patterns from GANs'. Both do this by practice, in a sentence, without arguing a class definition.
What does NOT support the author: no source found says that a morph detector must not be penalised for flagging a reconstruction, and Colbois and Marcel (BIOSIG 2022, IJCB 2024) openly propose treating deep-morph detection as synthetic-image detection, with a GAN-image detector giving near perfect results on GAN morphs. Unified face-attack benchmarks simply omit morphing. The fair statement for the paper is: neighbouring fields label reconstructions as fake by trace, the biometrics taxonomy keeps morphing separate from synthesis, MAD datasets quietly use generated or reconstructed one-identity images as bona fide, and nobody has stated the rule or measured it. That is a gap the paper can name and fill.

Q2, same-person morphs and one-image self-morphs. This body of literature is almost silent. Nothing found on mirror self-morphs or same-person morphs. Tolosana et al. and the Handbook define morphing by purpose ('resemble the biometric information of two or more individuals'), which does not settle a same-person or one-image case either way; read literally by purpose it would exclude them, read by process it says nothing. The only process-based precedent is self-blending: SBI (deepfakes) and SelfMAD (MAD) label a one-image self-blend as fake or pseudo-morph, but only as training surrogates, never as an evaluation class, and without arguing that such an image is an attack. So for Q2 the neighbouring fields give one weak precedent for 'the process defines the class' and one definitional phrase that leans the other way; there is no stand.
not_found: No paper found, in generated-image detection or deepfake detection, that states a rule for how a morph detector should treat a one-photo GAN or diffusion reconstruction, or that reports morph-detector error on such images as a defined metric.

No generated-image detection paper found that puts pure VAE or diffusion reconstructions of real photos in the REAL class for training. The 'real' framing appears only where the reconstruction is described as an attack, laundering or a codec (Cozzolino et al.; Cannas et al.; Mandelli et al.).

No benchmark or detector found that is evaluated jointly on morph detection and synthetic-face detection with a shared label policy. UniAttackData and UniAttackData+ (HiPTune) do not include morphing attacks.
Nothing found in these fields on same-person morphs or mirror self-morphs (Q2). Only self-blended training surrogates (SBI, SelfMAD).
Springer chapter pages for the Handbook could not be opened (login redirect); the open-access OAPEN PDF of the same book was read instead.
MagNet (Agarwal et al., 2021, digital presentation attacks including morphing and swapping) was seen only as a search result; the PMC page did not load. Not checked.

Venues not verified this session: Fake or JPEG (ECCVW 2024 per our notes), Chai et al. (ECCV 2020), AutoGAN (WIFS 2019), Mandelli et al. laundering paper, Stay-Positive, Cannas et al. JPEG AI paper, DiFF, SIDA (CVPR 2025), Zhang et al. arXiv 2501.09817 (CVPRW 2024 per our notes), Tolosana et al. journal version (Information Fusion 2020), UniAttackData (IJCAI 2024). Aligned Datasets ICLR 2025 rests on a proceedings URL in search results that was not opened. Cozzolino et al. venue rests on the citation in Mandelli et al.

SMDD and Colbois and Marcel (BIOSIG 2022) were searched by pattern, not read end to end, so 'no discussion of the label question' and 'no reconstructed bona fide control' mean no match was found, not a full-text guarantee.
ISO/IEC and NIST definitions of bona fide and morph were outside this topic and were not searched.

findings.claim: SMDD builds its bona fide class from 25k StyleGAN2-ADA faces sampled from random noise that 'will not go into a morphing process'. The stated logic is that a MAD detects the change the morphing process makes, and that this change should also be visible between synthetic images before and after morphing. The paper never discusses that a detector trained this way must then accept generated faces as genuine, and it has no passage on a synthetic versus real bona fide gap (zero hits for 'domain' and 'real bona fide' in the full text). It also says the SMDD morphs themselves are not a real attack because they are synthetic.
findings.source: Damer, Lopez, Fang, Spiller, Pham, Boutros. Privacy-friendly Synthetic Data for the Development of Face Morphing Attack Detectors. CVPR Workshops 2022. arXiv:2203.06691 (read on ar5iv)
findings.quote: MAD solutions are trained to detect the changes that the morphing process introduces to the image [...] This detectable difference, therefore, might be detectable as well between synthetic images before and after undergoing a morphing process. || the first will be considered the BF samples, namely the 25k-BF, and will not go into a morphing process || the SMDD is not presented as an attack (as it is based on synthetic data) and thus detecting it is not of interest
findings.bears_on: Q1: in practice a fully generated single-identity face is labelled bona fide; the class boundary is 'went through morphing or not', not 'generated or not'. Supports the author's lean by practice, but the paper is silent on the consequence. Q2: weak support for 'process defines the morph'.

findings.claim: SYN-MAD 2022 restricted training to the synthetic SMDD data (25k synthetic bona fide, 15k synthetic morphs) and tested on MAD22, whose bona fide class is 204 real FRLL photos. The report does not discuss the mismatch between synthetic training bona fides and real test bona fides, and does not discuss detectors keying on synthetic artefacts.
findings.source: Huber et al. SYN-MAD 2022: Competition on Face Morphing Attack Detection Based on Privacy-aware Synthetic Training Data. IJCB 2022. arXiv:2208.07337 (read on ar5iv through the fetch tool; quotes are as returned by its summariser)
findings.quote: consists of 25k bona fide and 15k morphing images based on synthetic faces || and 204 bona fide images from the FRLL dataset
findings.bears_on: Q1: synthetic single-identity faces are bona fide by protocol; explicit silence on whether detectors must accept generated faces. Q2: silent.

findings.claim: SynMorph states the generator shortcut openly: training an S-MAD on real bona fides plus MIPGAN morphs lets the model separate GAN-generated from non-synthetic images instead of learning morphing traces. Their fix is to use as the non-morphed class real images reconstructed with the same StyleGAN2 generator as MIPGAN-II. So a one-photo GAN reconstruction is placed in the non-morphed (bona fide) class. They also note that landmark morphs of GAN-generated faces may carry GAN traces, that training on synthetic and testing on real gives high error, and they recommend careful reporting when synthetic data is used to evaluate MAD.
findings.source: Zhang, Ramachandra, Raja, Busch. SynMorph: Generating Synthetic Face Morphing Dataset with Mated Samples. IEEE Access 2025 (DOI 10.1109/ACCESS.2025.3548957). arXiv:2409.05595, Section V
findings.quote: using MIPGAN-based morphs as training data usually makes it easy for the model to overfit on the determination between GAN-generated images and non-synthetic images instead of learning the traces of morphing [...] we used reconstructed non-morphed images with the same backbone StyleGAN2 generator as MIPGAN-II to mitigate the bias between non-morphed non-synthetic images and morphed non-synthetic images. || it is suggested to carefully report when using synthetic data for evaluating MAD.
findings.bears_on: Q1: strongest direct support for the author's lean. A one-image GAN reconstruction is treated as non-morphed, and detecting 'GAN versus real' is called overfitting, not morph detection. It is a training trick, not a stated definition, and no false alarm rate on reconstructions is reported. Q2: silent.

findings.claim: The same NTNU group states the goal explicitly in their ViT S-MAD paper: the detector should learn morphing patterns, not general GAN patterns, so reconstructed bona fide images are used in the datasets built with GAN morphing algorithms (StyleGAN-IWBF, MIPGAN-I, MIPGAN-II). No separate measurement of false alarms on those reconstructions versus untouched bona fides is given.
findings.source: Zhang, Ramachandra, Raja, Busch. Generalized Single-Image-Based Morphing Attack Detection Using Deep Representations from Vision Transformer. arXiv:2501.09817 (Jan 2025; venue not verified). Section 3, read from the PDF
findings.quote: As our target is to train the model to learn patterns generated from morphing instead of general patterns from GANs, reconstructed bona fide images are applied to the datasets with GAN-based morphing algorithms. In this way, we can reduce the bias between bona fide and morph samples
findings.bears_on: Q1: supports the author's lean. One-photo GAN reconstruction equals bona fide, and GAN-pattern detection is treated as a bias to remove. Q2: silent, but the introduction defines a morph as combining samples 'from 2 or more individuals'.

findings.claim: Colbois and Marcel take the opposite position for GAN morphs. A generic GAN-image detector (ResNet50 trained on ProGAN, used out of the box) beat every dedicated detector on StyleGAN2 and MIPGAN morphs, and they conclude that deep-morph detection is 'strongly equivalent' to GAN-image detection. Bona fides are the untouched source photos; there is no one-identity reconstruction control (zero hits for 'reconstruct').
findings.source: Colbois, Marcel. On the detection of morphing attacks generated by GANs. BIOSIG 2022 (DOI 10.1109/BIOSIG55365.2022.9897046). arXiv:2209.00404
findings.quote: It thus looks like simply reusing a GAN-image detector is currently the most effective way to approach deep-MAD. || This seems to confirm the problematic of deep-MAD is strongly equivalent to the one of GAN-image detection
findings.bears_on: Q1: against the author's lean. This paper merges generated-image detection and MAD for deep morphs. Under this view a one-photo GAN reconstruction would be flagged and that would count as success. The paper does not test or discuss that case.

findings.claim: The same authors later made this a stated programme: treat MAD as a deepfake or synthetic-image detection problem, using features from large models pretrained on real data, with supervised probes and one-class models of the bona fide class. Morph sets include MorDIFF and StyleGAN2 morphs; bona fides are real FRLL, FRGC and FFHQ photos. No single-identity generated control is included (zero hits for 'non-morph', 'single identity').
findings.source: Colbois, Marcel. Evaluating the Effectiveness of Attack-Agnostic Features for Morphing Attack Detection. IJCB 2024 (DOI 10.1109/IJCB62174.2024.10744532). arXiv:2410.16802
findings.quote: We propose to consider the reverse perspective: treating MAD as a deepfake detection problem, specifically focusing on detecting deep synthetic images.
findings.bears_on: Q1: against the author's lean, explicit. A one-class 'real photo' model would by design reject any generated or reconstructed single-identity face. Q2: silent, but the introduction defines the attack as merging 'two distinct source identities'.

findings.claim: In the template-inversion morph paper the detectability argument is that the morph is 'in the end a particular output of a StyleGAN model', and detectability is measured with a generic GAN-image detector against 1000 real FFHQ images as the bona fide set. A single-face template inversion (reconstruction of one identity) is the core building block of the method but is never scored by a detector.
findings.source: Colbois, Shahreza, Marcel. Approximating Optimal Morphing Attacks using Template Inversion. IJCB 2023 (DOI 10.1109/IJCB57857.2023.10448752). arXiv:2402.00695, Section 4.3
findings.quote: GAN-inversion morphs in particular are still in the end a particular output of a StyleGAN model. StyleGAN images can be reliably detected
findings.bears_on: Q1: against the author's lean in practice (generator trace used as the morph cue); silent on one-identity reconstructions as a test class.

findings.claim: MIPGAN uses real FRGC photos as bona fide, applies the same print-scan and compression to both classes, and has no GAN reconstruction of a single bona fide face in its detection experiments. It attributes the easy detection of StyleGAN and MIPGAN morphs to GAN-synthesised noise, that is, to a generator trace, without discussing that this is not evidence of morphing.
findings.source: Zhang, Venkatesh, Ramachandra, Raja, Damer, Busch. MIPGAN - Generating Strong and High Quality Morphing Attacks Using Identity Prior Driven GAN. IEEE TBIOM 3(3), 2021. arXiv:2009.01729 (read on ar5iv)
findings.quote: The attack images created using StyleGAN and proposed MIPGAN can be efficiently detected using both the employed approaches with high accuracy. This can be attributed to the noises that are synthesised using GANs due to the computational modifications performed on the latent space in GAN-based morph generation methods.
findings.bears_on: Q1: the authors themselves say detectors pick up generator noise, yet no one-identity control is run. Silence on how a reconstruction should be labelled (the later NTNU papers above fill this in).

findings.claim: MorDIFF scores detectability against the 204 real FRLL bona fide images of SYN-MAD 2022 with MADs trained on SMDD, LMA-DRD and MorGAN-LMA. There is no encode-decode of a single face through the diffusion autoencoder as a control. Generative artefacts are discussed only as visual appearance (GAN 'streaking' present in MIPGAN, 'almost non-existent' in MorDIFF).
findings.source: Damer, Fang, Siebke, Kolf, Huber, Boutros. MorDIFF: Recognition Vulnerability and Attack Detectability of Face Morphing Attacks Created by Diffusion Autoencoders. IWBF 2023. arXiv:2302.01843 (read on ar5iv)
findings.quote: in total 1000 MorDIFF attack images and the 204 bona fide images of the SYN-MAD 2022 dataset || For most MADs, the MorDIFF was not the most, nor the least accurately detected morph type.
findings.bears_on: Q1: explicit silence. No one-identity diffusion reconstruction, no statement on whether detectors see morphing or the diffusion decoder.

findings.claim: The DiM family (DiM, Fast-DiM, Greedy-DiM) runs S-MAD detectability studies with an SE-ResNeXt101 detector on SYN-MAD 2022 data and real bona fides. None includes a one-identity reconstruction as a control or as a bona fide class. Fast-DiM does reconstruct single FRLL images through the diffusion autoencoder, but only to report LPIPS and MSE fidelity of the forward ODE solver, not to score them with a detector. DiM says the diffusion attack is hard to detect as a novel attack because of 'its unique morph generation process'.
findings.source: Blasingame, Liu. Leveraging Diffusion For Strong and High Quality Face Morphing Attacks, IEEE TBIOM 6(1) 2024, arXiv:2301.04218; Fast-DiM: Towards Fast Diffusion Morphs, IEEE Security and Privacy 2024, arXiv:2310.09484; Greedy-DiM, IJCB 2024, arXiv:2404.06025
findings.quote: Fast-DiM: 'we measure the LPIPS metric and Mean Squared Error (MSE) between the original and reconstructed images from the FRLL dataset.' DiM: 'the Diffusion attack is very difficult to detect as a novel attack, which can at least be partially attributed to its unique morph generation process'
findings.bears_on: Q1: explicit silence. Reconstructions exist in the pipeline but are never used to separate 'diffusion trace' from 'morphing'. Greedy-DiM checked through the fetch summariser only.

findings.claim: ReGenMorph (landmark morph re-generated through a GAN) evaluates detectability against real FRGC bona fides. It does not re-generate a non-morphed image as a control, although the method itself is a one-image GAN pass applied to an already morphed image.
findings.source: Damer, Raja, Suessmilch, Venkatesh, Boutros, Fang, Kirchbuchner, Ramachandra, Kuijper. ReGenMorph: Visibly Realistic GAN Generated Face Morphing Attacks by Attack Re-generation. ISVC 2021. arXiv:2108.09130 (read on ar5iv through the fetch tool; quote as returned by its summariser)
findings.quote: to eliminate the LMA blending artifacts by using a GAN-based generation.
findings.bears_on: Q1: silence. The natural control (GAN re-generation of a genuine photo) is missing.

findings.claim: LADIMO, MorCode and Morph-PIPE contain no detectability experiment at all; they report vulnerability or attack potential only. In LADIMO the phrase 'bona fide' does not occur in the text. So they say nothing on what a detector should do with a one-identity output of the same generator.
findings.source: Grimmer, Busch. LADIMO, arXiv:2410.07988 (2024). PN, Ramachandra, Venkatesh, Rao, Mitra, Krishna. MorCode, arXiv:2410.07625 (2024). Zhang, Ramachandra, Raja, Busch. Morph-PIPE, NIKT/NISK 2023, https://www.ntnu.no/ojs/index.php/nikt/article/view/5649 (PDF read)
findings.bears_on: Q1: silence (no detection study). Q2: silence.

findings.claim: Tapia and Busch report that training only on synthetic bona fide and synthetic morphs (SYN-MAD data) is not enough to detect real digital morphs, and that a mix with real images is needed; their best result used at least 20 percent real images. They frame this as a data shortfall, not as a class-definition problem, and do not ask whether the detector should accept generated faces.
findings.source: Tapia, Busch. Impact of Synthetic Images on Morphing Attack Detection Using a Siamese Network. CIARP 2023 (arXiv version). arXiv:2403.09380
findings.quote: using only synthetic images as bona fice and morph is still not enough to detect real MAD based on digital images. || The best results were obtained when at least 20% of the images belonged to digital faces (no synthetic).
findings.bears_on: Q1: synthetic single-identity faces are accepted as bona fide without comment; evidence of a synthetic to real gap; silent on the definitional question.

findings.claim: Tapia, Russo and Busch pass both bona fide and morphed images through Pix2pix and CycleGAN to synthesise print-scan texture, and keep the original labels. A genuine photo transformed by a GAN (one image in, one image out) stays bona fide.
findings.source: Tapia, Russo, Busch. Generating Automatically Print/Scan Textures for Morphing Attack Detection Applications. arXiv:2408.09558 (2024, 'under revision process in Journal')
findings.quote: both the pairing and unpairing methods can generate synthetic images to create and transfer the style from printed/scanned images applied to bona fide and morphed face images.
findings.bears_on: Q1: supports the author's lean by practice. One-image generative processing does not change the bona fide label. No false alarm study on such images.

findings.claim: NIST FATE MORPH defines morphing as blending two or more subjects' faces, defines BSCER on 'bona fide (nonmorph)' samples, and uses only live-capture mugshot and visa photos (plus printed and scanned non-morphs) as bona fides. The report contains no synthetic, GAN-reconstructed, retouched or AI-enhanced single-identity test set (zero hits for 'synthetic', 'retouch', 'reconstruct' in the full text). It does report that detectors flag processed genuine photos: many algorithms classify most printed-and-scanned photos as morphs.
findings.source: Ngan, Grother, Hanaoka, Kuo. NISTIR 8292 Draft Supplement, FATE Part 4: MORPH, report dated 14 September 2026. https://pages.nist.gov/frvt/reports/morph/frvt_morph_report.pdf (PDF text read)
findings.quote: Face morphing is an image manipulation technique where two or more subjects' faces are morphed or blended together to form a single face in a photograph. || BSCER is defined as the proportion of bona fide (nonmorph) samples incorrectly classified as morphed samples. || very high false detection rates, which means the algorithms are classifying most scanned photos as morphs, even when they're not.
findings.bears_on: Q1: bona fide means 'nonmorph'; silent on generated or reconstructed one-identity images, which are simply not tested. Shows that false alarms on processed genuine photos are a recognised failure. Q2: the definition needs two or more subjects, which by wording excludes a same-person or mirror self-morph; NIST does not discuss the case.

findings.claim: The da/sec handbook chapter treats face manipulation detection as 'bona fide or manipulated' and separates manipulations by security effect: morphs let attackers circumvent the system, while slight retouching by bona fide users has little to no security implication. It does not say how a morph detector should treat a retouched genuine photo.
findings.source: Ibsen, Rathgeb, Fischer, Drozdowski, Busch. Digital Face Manipulation in Biometric Systems. Handbook of Digital Face Manipulation and Detection, Springer 2022, chapter 2. https://link.springer.com/chapter/10.1007/978-3-030-87664-7_2
findings.quote: some manipulations (e.g. morphed images) [...] can be used by attackers to circumvent the security of the system, whereas other manipulations usually carried out by bona fide users like slight retouching has little to no security implications
findings.bears_on: Q1 (beautified or enhanced photos): the literature separates morphing from benign single-identity editing by security effect, which supports not counting such edits as attacks; but in the generic detector framing here a retouched image is 'manipulated', not 'bona fide'. No rule for S-MAD.

findings.claim: The one MAD paper found that touches beautification uses a beauty score as a morph cue (hypothesis: bona fide faces are 'less beautiful', morphs are smoother) and only raises, without testing, the question of what beautified images do to morph detection. It reports no false alarm rate on beautified genuine photos.
findings.source: Tapia, Ibsen, Busch. Beauty Score Fusion for Morphing Attack Detection. BMVC 2024 workshop (SRBS). https://bmva-archive.org.uk/bmvc/2024/workshops/SRBS/0006.pdf (PDF text read)
findings.quote: Our finding raised the question of the impact of beautifying images and their effects on evading morph detection.
findings.bears_on: Q1 (beautified or AI-enhanced genuine photos): open question in the literature; a smoothness cue of this kind would be expected to flag beautified genuine photos, but nobody measured it.

findings.claim: Older MAD work recognised pipeline shortcuts but handled them by equal classical processing of both classes, not by one-identity generative controls. Scherhag et al. post-process bona fide and morphed images in the same ways (resize, JPEG2000, print-scan) and warn about overfitting to algorithm and database specific artefacts. Seibold et al. add noise and blur to genuine images and morphs alike. Spreeuwers et al. say a detector trained on one dataset may only detect a property of the morph creation process, and show noise or rescaling of morphs breaks it. In Seibold et al. 2019, style transfer, sharpening and histogram equalisation are applied to morphs only, never to genuine images.
findings.source: Scherhag, Rathgeb, Merkle, Busch, Deep Face Representations for Differential Morphing Attack Detection, arXiv:2001.01202. Seibold, Samek, Hilsmann, Eisert, arXiv:1806.04265 (through fetch summariser). Seibold, Hilsmann, Eisert, Style Your Face Morph..., BIOSIG 2019, arXiv:2004.11435. Spreeuwers, Schils, Veldhuis, Kelly, Practical Evaluation of Face Morphing Attack Detection Methods, Springer handbook 2022, chapter 16
findings.quote: Scherhag: 'the passport images (bona fide and morphed) of the MAD database are post-processed in different manners.' Spreeuwers: 'This may result in a morphing attack detection method that only detects a certain property of the morphing creation process.'
findings.bears_on: Q1: the principle 'do not let processing history separate the classes' is old and accepted, which backs the author's lean in spirit. None of these papers extends it to GAN or diffusion reconstructions, or measures false alarms on enhanced genuine photos.

findings.claim: Two works from Coimbra use same-person morphs ('selfmorphs', two different photos of one identity put through the morphing tool) and label them bona fide, with the stated aim of stopping the detector from learning pipeline artefacts instead of identity mixing. They credit Borghi et al. for introducing selfmorphing (there used to create artefacts for a retouching GAN). MorphGuard applies this with landmark, StyleGAN and diffusion-autoencoder morphing.
findings.source: Medvedev, Shadmand, Goncalves. MorDeephy: Face Morphing Detection Via Fused Classification. arXiv:2208.03110 (2022; venue not verified), Section 4.3. Medvedev, Goncalves. MorphGuard: Morph Specific Margin Loss for Enhancing Robustness to Face Morphing Attacks. arXiv:2505.10497 (2025; venue not verified), Section V-B
findings.quote: MorDeephy: 'we utilize selfmorph images to focus morphing detection onto the deep face features behaviour, rather than to detecting artefacts. [...] we consider selfmorphs as bona fide samples.' MorphGuard: 'selfmorphs are treated as bona fide samples'
findings.bears_on: Q2: against the author's lean. These authors label a same-person morph bona fide even though the morphing method was used. Q1: same logic as the reconstruction controls (artefacts of the method are not the attack). Found outside my assigned topic; a mirror-image (one photo) variant was not seen in either paper.

findings.claim: SelfMAD goes the other way on self-blends and is silent on synthetic bona fides. It trains only on the 25k SMDD StyleGAN2 bona fide images, creates pseudo-morphs by blending an image with a transformed copy of itself plus frequency artefacts, and labels those as attacks. It tests on real bona fides (FRGC, FERET, FRLL) and does not discuss that its bona fide training class is entirely GAN-generated.
findings.source: Ivanovska, Todorov, Damer, Jain, Peer, Struc. SelfMAD: Enhancing Generalization and Robustness in Morphing Attack Detection via Self-Supervised Learning. FG 2025. arXiv:2504.05504 (HTML read; label values are in stripped maths, wording around them was seen)
findings.quote: For training SelfMAD, we use [...] || By leveraging a diverse set of synthetic artifacts, the classifier learns to identify general features indicative of morphing attacks rather than overfitting to characteristics of specific morphing techniques.
findings.bears_on: Q2: a one-image self-blend is labelled attack, but as a training surrogate for real morphs, not as a definitional claim. Consistent in outcome with the author's lean, for a different reason. Q1: synthetic bona fides used without comment.

not_found: No MAD paper was found that reports a false alarm rate (BPCER or BSCER) on GAN-reconstructed, diffusion-reconstructed, super-resolved or AI-enhanced genuine photos as a test condition. Three web searches aimed at this returned nothing; the closest items are the NTNU training-time reconstructions (SynMorph, ViT S-MAD), which report no separate error on the reconstructions.

No GAN or diffusion morphing paper among MIPGAN, ReGenMorph, MorDIFF, DiM, Fast-DiM, Greedy-DiM includes a one-identity control (inversion or encode-decode of a single face) in its detectability study. LADIMO, MorCode and Morph-PIPE have no detectability study at all.

No source was found that states in so many words that generated-image detection and S-MAD are different tasks and that a morph detector should not be penalised for accepting generated one-identity faces. The NTNU papers imply it; Colbois and Marcel state the opposite for GAN morphs.

No published critique of SMDD or SYN-MAD 2022 was found for using fully generated faces as bona fide, and neither source discusses that a detector trained on them must accept generated faces. The SMDD paper has no domain-gap passage.

No statement was found in NIST FATE MORPH on synthetic, reconstructed or retouched single-identity images; the report text has zero hits for 'synthetic', 'retouch' and 'reconstruct'. The NIST web page itself was too large to fetch; the report PDF was read instead.

Di Domenico, Borghi, Franco, Maltoni, Face Restoration for Morphed Images Retouching (IWBF 2024, CodeFormer applied to morphs): could not be opened (HTTP 403 from the UNIBO repository). Whether restoration was also applied to bona fide images, and how detectors reacted, is not verified.

MorGAN (Damer et al., BTAS 2018) and Realistic Dreams (Damer et al., BTAS 2019, super-resolution of GAN morphs) are behind the IEEE paywall and were not opened. Whether either has a reconstruction or enhancement control on bona fide images is not verified.

Kraetzer, Makrushin, Neubert, Hildebrandt, Dittmann, Modeling Attacks on Photo-ID Documents (IH&MMSec 2017), which from memory models legitimate editing steps in the photo-ID life cycle, was not opened. Not verified.
ISO/IEC 20059 term entries (morph, bona fide) were not opened in this pass; only NIST's wording aligned to that standard was read.

Borghi et al., Automated Artifact Retouching in Morphed Images with Attention Maps (IEEE Access 2021), cited by MorDeephy and MorphGuard as the origin of selfmorphing, was not opened; its labelling of selfmorphs is known only through those two citing papers.
A mirror self-morph (one photo morphed with its own mirror image) was not seen in any source opened in this pass.
stance_summary:
Q1 (one-photo reconstructions, synthetic single-identity faces, enhanced photos). The MAD literature has no stated rule, but it has a clear working practice and one open disagreement.

Practice: wherever a single-identity generated or generatively processed image appears in a MAD dataset, it is labelled bona fide. SMDD and SYN-MAD 2022 use fully generated StyleGAN2 faces as the bona fide class (the class boundary is 'went through the morphing process or not'). Tapia, Russo and Busch pass genuine photos through Pix2pix or CycleGAN print-scan simulation and keep them bona fide. Most directly, the NTNU group (SynMorph, IEEE Access 2025; ViT S-MAD, arXiv 2501.09817) reconstructs genuine photos with the same StyleGAN2 generator used by MIPGAN and uses them as the non-morphed class, and says why: otherwise the model learns 'GAN-generated versus non-synthetic' instead of 'the traces of morphing'. That is the closest thing to a published stand, and it agrees with the author's lean. It is a training trick in a dataset section, not a definition, and no paper reports false alarms on such reconstructions.

Disagreement: Colbois and Marcel (BIOSIG 2022, IJCB 2023, IJCB 2024) argue that detection of GAN morphs is 'strongly equivalent' to GAN-image detection and propose 'treating MAD as a deepfake detection problem'. Under that view a one-photo reconstruction would be flagged and counted as a hit. They never test or discuss the one-identity case. MIPGAN also attributes detection to GAN noise without drawing a conclusion.

Silence: none of the GAN or diffusion morph generation papers checked (MIPGAN, ReGenMorph, MorDIFF, DiM, Fast-DiM, Greedy-DiM) runs a one-identity reconstruction control in its detectability study, and LADIMO, MorCode and Morph-PIPE have no detection study. SMDD and SYN-MAD do not discuss that their detectors must accept generated faces. NIST FATE MORPH defines bona fide as 'nonmorph', tests only live-capture photos, and has no synthetic, reconstructed or retouched single-identity set. No paper was found that measures false alarms on GAN-reconstructed, diffusion-reconstructed, super-resolved or AI-enhanced genuine photos. On beautification the literature separates it from morphing by security effect (Ibsen et al. 2022) and one workshop paper raises the question without answering it. So the paper can truthfully say: practice treats such images as bona fide, one group gives the reason, another group merges the two tasks, and nobody has measured it or defined it.

Q2 (same-person morphs, one-image self-morphs). This was outside my topic, but what I met is split and mostly definitional by implication. Definitions (NIST, the ViT S-MAD introduction, Colbois and Marcel, Tapia and Busch) all require two or more different subjects, which by wording excludes a same-person morph, but none discusses the case. Two Coimbra papers (MorDeephy, MorphGuard) explicitly label same-person 'selfmorphs' as bona fide, to stop the detector learning tool artefacts; that is against the author's lean. SelfMAD labels one-image self-blends as attacks, but as a surrogate for real morphs during training, not as a claim about what a morph is. I found no source that takes the position 'if the morphing method is used, it is a morph' as a definition, and no source on a mirror self-morph. The SMDD rationale (the detector looks for what the morphing process changes) is the nearest support for the author's reading.

Caveats: quotes were taken from text extracted from arXiv HTML, ar5iv, Springer pages or PDFs this session; items marked as read through the fetch summariser carry short quotes as that tool returned them. Maths was stripped in extraction. Venues marked 'not verified' had no venue on the arXiv page.

findings.claim: ICAO Doc 9303 Part 2 defines morphing only by its content: faces of two or more subjects blended into one. It says nothing about a blend of two photos of one subject or of one photo with a transformed copy. Read literally, a one-subject self-morph is not 'morphing' under this definition.
findings.source: ICAO Doc 9303, Machine Readable Travel Documents, Eighth Edition 2021, Part 2 (Security of the Design, Manufacture and Issuance of MRTDs), list of fraud types. https://www.icao.int/sites/default/files/publications/DocSeries/9303_p2_cons_en.pdf (edition served on icao.int on 2026-11-11; whether a newer edition exists was not verified)
findings.quote: Morphing is an image manipulation technique where two or more subjects’ faces are morphed or blended together to form a single face in a photograph.
findings.bears_on: Q2: definition is by number of subjects, not by the tool used; leans against 'method used means morph' on a literal reading, but the case is not addressed. Q1: silent.

findings.claim: ICAO Doc 9303 Part 3 section 3.9.1 sets a separate, broader rule for the portrait: it must be a true likeness and must not be digitally altered or enhanced to change appearance. This rule does not use the word morphing. So for the issuing authority, an appearance-changing reconstruction, beautification or self-blend is a non-compliant portrait, without being called a morph.
findings.source: ICAO Doc 9303, Eighth Edition 2021, Part 3 (Specifications Common to all MRTDs), section 3.9.1 Displayed facial image. https://www.icao.int/sites/default/files/publications/DocSeries/9303_p3_cons_en.pdf
findings.quote: depict a true likeness of the rightful holder of the MRTD; and not be digitally altered or enhanced to change the subject’s appearance in any way.
findings.bears_on: Q1: supports keeping 'digitally altered single-subject image' as a category distinct from 'morph'; but it does NOT make such an image an acceptable (bona fide) portrait. Q2: a self-morph that changes appearance would be a prohibited alteration, yet ICAO does not label it morphing.

findings.claim: The ICAO Technical Report on Portrait Quality (authored by ISO/IEC JTC1 SC17 WG3) gives a closed list of admissible post-acquisition processing (in-plane rotation, cropping, down sampling, white balance, ICC colour management, one RAW conversion, compression) and forbids local modification of the face. It names 'photo manipulation' and 'morphing' as two separate risks. GAN inversion or diffusion re-encoding is not on the admissible list; the report does not mention synthetic or reconstructed images at all.
findings.source: ICAO Technical Report: Portrait Quality (Reference Facial Images for MRTD), Version 1.0, April 2018, clauses 4.4 and 9.4. https://www.icao.int/sites/default/files/TRIP/Publications/TR-Portrait-Quality-v1.0.pdf
findings.quote: the risks of photo manipulation and morphing inherent with such an uncontrolled process are suitably mitigated. [...] The face images shall not be modified locally, e.g., for removal of scars, pimples or other skin impurities or to modify the shape or location of the nose, the eyes, the eyebrows or any other facial landmarks.
findings.bears_on: Q1: manipulation and morphing are separate named risks (supports task separation), but a one-photo reconstruction would be inadmissible processing, not a clean bona fide portrait. Q2: silent on same-subject morphs.

findings.claim: ISO/IEC 20059:2025 (the morphing evaluation standard) frames a morphing attack by its identity outcome: references manipulated to match two or more data subjects, a 'multiple identity attack'. Its scope says it defines 'biometric sample modifications and manipulation' with a focus on those that constitute a multiple identity attack. Only the Foreword, Introduction, Scope and term 3.1 (image content) were readable in the free preview; the remaining terms (clause 3), clause 5 'Morphing attacks' and clause 7 'Morph detection error rates' are paywalled and were not read.
findings.source: ISO/IEC 20059:2025, Information technology - Methodologies to evaluate the resistance of biometric systems to morphing attacks, First edition 2025-08, preview pages. https://assets.vde-verlag.de/iec-normen/preview-pdf/info_isoiec20059%7Bed1.0%7Den.pdf (table of contents also confirmed in the DIN preview)
findings.quote: morphing attacks, where biometric references are manipulated to match two or more biometric data subjects submitted during enrolment, pose a threat to image-based biometric systems (BSs). [...] a definition of biometric sample modifications and manipulation with a specific focus on manipulations that constitute a multiple identity attack.
findings.bears_on: Q2: the standard's attack concept needs two or more data subjects; a same-person or mirror self-morph is not a multiple identity attack. Whether clause 3 or 5 classifies single-subject modifications could not be verified. Q1: not answered in the readable part.

findings.claim: ISO/IEC 30107-1:2023 states that morphing attacks are outside the presentation attack detection series, and defines them again as samples manipulated to match two or more data subjects. Its PAD vocabulary puts 'synthetic biometric patterns' under the term 'artefact', that is, in the presentation attack family, not in the morphing family.
findings.source: ISO/IEC 30107-1:2023, Biometric presentation attack detection - Part 1: Framework, Introduction and terms 3.1, iTeh sample. https://cdn.standards.iteh.ai/samples/83828/8ff61d4f89f74b8eb27f110eba29e70f/ISO-IEC-30107-1-2023.pdf
findings.quote: Morphing attacks, where biometric samples that are manipulated to match two or more biometric data subjects are submitted during enrolment, are not considered in the ISO/IEC 30107 series, though the performance assessment methods are similar for PAD and morphing attack detection mechanisms.
findings.bears_on: Q1: ISO keeps morphing detection and other attack detection in separate standards; synthetic patterns are handled in the PAD vocabulary (weak support for task separation, since PAD concerns the capture device). Q2: two or more data subjects again.

findings.claim: NIST FATE MORPH (current report) defines morphing as blending two or more subjects' faces, states that all tested morphs are made from two subjects, and glosses the negative class as 'bona fide (nonmorph)'. The bona fide data are real photographs only: the source images of the morphs, about 1 million live-capture mugshots, about 872K live-capture visa images, and a printed-and-scanned subset. A full-text search of the report found no occurrence of 'synthetic', 'StyleGAN', 'retouch', 'beautif' or 'self-morph'. There are no single-subject synthetic, reconstructed or same-subject-morph images in either class.
findings.source: Ngan, Grother, Hanaoka, Kuo, NISTIR 8292 Draft Supplement, Face Analysis Technology Evaluation (FATE) Part 4: MORPH - Performance of Automated Face Morph Detection, last updated September 14, 2026. https://pages.nist.gov/frvt/reports/morph/frvt_morph_report.pdf (sections 2.3, 3.1, 3.2, 4.1.1, Tables 5 to 7)
findings.quote: BSCER is defined as the proportion of bona fide (nonmorph) samples incorrectly classified as morphed samples. [...] All morphs are created with two subjects and subject alpha, where known, is 0.5
findings.bears_on: Q1: NIST is silent; its bona fide class is live captures (plus print-scan), so it neither penalises nor exempts detectors on one-photo reconstructions. The gloss 'bona fide (nonmorph)' implies a binary where anything that is not a morph sits on the bona fide side, but NIST never tests that. Q2: silent; same-subject morphs are not in the test.

findings.claim: NIST treats a processed genuine photo as bona fide: printed-and-scanned non-morphs are in the bona fide class, and a detector that flags them is reported as making false detections.
findings.source: Ngan, Grother, Hanaoka, Kuo, NISTIR 8292, Face Recognition Vendor Test (FRVT) Part 4: MORPH - Performance of Automated Face Morph Detection, March 2020, Executive Summary. https://nvlpubs.nist.gov/nistpubs/ir/2020/NIST.IR.8292.pdf (same wording kept in the 2026 draft supplement)
findings.quote: For a majority of the algorithms, morph miss rates are low BUT false detection rates are extremely high, so the algorithms appear to be classifying most scanned photos as morphs, even when they’re not.
findings.bears_on: Q1: closest official precedent by analogy. A single-subject image that went through a heavy but identity-neutral process (print and scan) is bona fide and flagging it is a false alarm. NIST does not extend this to GAN or diffusion reconstructions.

findings.claim: The NIST FATE MORPH evaluation plan describes the task as detecting 'a morphed/blended image of two or more faces' and, for the demorphing track, specifies that a bona fide input should yield two outputs that are essentially the same as the input. In this specification the bona fide case is exactly the case where both recovered identities coincide.
findings.source: Ngan, Grother, Hanaoka, FATE MORPH: Concept, Evaluation Plan and API, Version 5.0.2, August 16, 2024, sections 1.4 and 5.3.8. https://pages.nist.gov/frvt/api/FRVT_ongoing_morph_api.pdf
findings.quote: All morphs will be generated with two contributing subjects, and both morphed and non-morphed images will be evaluated. [...] If the input is a bona fide image, the algorithm should produce two images/identities that are essentially the same as the input photo.
findings.bears_on: Q2: by NIST's operational logic a blend whose two contributors are the same identity behaves like a bona fide, not like a morph (inference from the spec, not a statement by NIST). Q1: silent.

findings.claim: NIST's operational guideline defines a morphed photograph as a combination of two or more human faces and says morphing methods combine photos of two or more individuals. It calls the non-morph outcome of an investigation 'a legitimate photo'. It notes morphs may be touched up afterwards, but says nothing on same-person blends, synthetic faces or retouched genuine photos as a class.
findings.source: Ngan and Grother, NIST IR 8584, FATE MORPH 4B: Considerations for Implementing Morph Detection in Operations, August 2025. https://nvlpubs.nist.gov/nistpubs/ir/2025/NIST.IR.8584.pdf
findings.quote: A morphed photograph is a combination of two or more human faces into one photograph. [...] Morphing methods combine photos of two or more individuals. [...] An investigation, if successful, will reveal that this flagged photo is a morph or a legitimate photo i.e., a false detection.
findings.bears_on: Q2: multi-individual definition; silent on same-person morphs. Q1: silent.

findings.claim: The FVC-onGoing S-MAD benchmark area (University of Bologna; hosts the SOTAMD and iMARS sequestered benchmarks and accepts NIST FATE MORPH compliant libraries) defines the task as deciding whether an image results from 'mixing faces of two subjects'. Its bona fide sets are the genuine source photographs (digital or printed and scanned). Its metrics are BSCER and MACER; the companion Fi-DMAD page attributes them to ISO/IEC DIS 20059 (that attribution seen only through a paraphrasing fetch).
findings.source: FVC-onGoing, Benchmark area: Single-image Morph Attack Detection. https://biolab.csr.unibo.it/fvcongoing/UI/Form/BenchmarkAreas/BenchmarkAreaSMAD.aspx
findings.quote: Morphing detection consists in analyzing a face image to determine whether it is the result of a morphing process (mixing faces of two subjects) or not.
findings.bears_on: Q2: wording joins process and subject count ('morphing process (mixing faces of two subjects)'); a one-subject self-morph is not covered. Q1: bona fide means genuine photographs; no synthetic or reconstructed single-subject images.

findings.claim: In the SOTAMD benchmark the bona fide enrolment images are not raw captures: they were processed with professional software for ICAO compliance, cropped, resized to match the morphs' inter-eye distance, and partly printed and scanned. They remain bona fide.
findings.source: Raja, Ferrara, Franco, Spreeuwers, Batskos, de Wit, Gomez-Barrero, Scherhag, Fischer, Venkatesh, Singh et al., Morphing Attack Detection - Database, Evaluation Platform and Benchmarking, arXiv:2006.06458 (published in IEEE TIFS; year not verified), section 3.2. https://arxiv.org/pdf/2006.06458
findings.quote: each of the images in the enrolment set was processed with professional software to comply with ICAO standards for eMRTD images.
findings.bears_on: Q1: an EU-funded reference benchmark treats processed single-subject photographs as bona fide (processing alone does not move an image to the attack class). It does not cover generative reconstruction.

findings.claim: The same SOTAMD paper, describing the Face Demorphing baseline, states the modelling assumption that a genuine document image is a combination of two identical images. In this formalism a 'morph' of a subject with themself is the bona fide case.
findings.source: Raja et al., Morphing Attack Detection - Database, Evaluation Platform and Benchmarking, arXiv:2006.06458, section 5.1.6 Face demorphing. https://arxiv.org/pdf/2006.06458
findings.quote: The assumption on the other end is that for a genuine ID document (with no morphing attack) the image Im is a combination of two identical images (for e.g., Im = Ia + Ia ), where Ia is the bona fide image.
findings.bears_on: Q2: against 'method used means morph' within the demorphing formalism: self-combination equals bona fide. Caveat: it speaks of two identical images, not of two different photos of one person or a mirrored copy, so it does not settle those cases.

findings.claim: The standardisation-oriented methodology paper by the Darmstadt group with NIST, BSI, Bologna, Twente and Idiap co-authors defines a morphing attack as enrolling a sample merged from two or multiple subjects, states that a morphed sample is related to at least two subjects, and recommends equal quality for bona fide and morphed samples. It notes ISO/IEC 30107-3 metrics apply to one subject per attack and therefore need adapting.
findings.source: Scherhag, Nautsch, Rathgeb, Gomez-Barrero, Veldhuis, Spreeuwers, Schils, Maltoni, Grother, Marcel, Breithaupt et al., Biometric Systems under Morphing Attacks: Assessment of Morphing Techniques and Vulnerability Reporting, BIOSIG 2017 (LNI). https://www.christoph-busch.de/files/Scherhag-Methodology-BIOSIG-2017.pdf
findings.quote: It should be noted, that one morphed sample is related to at least two subjects and each subject might contribute to several morphing samples.
findings.bears_on: Q2: 'at least two subjects' is part of the definition used by the group that later drove ISO/IEC 20059; same-subject morphs are not discussed. Q1: the equal-quality recommendation supports matching the processing of bona fide to morphs, but says nothing on synthetic or reconstructed bona fide.

findings.claim: Morphing Attack Potential, the measure on which ISO/IEC 20059 is based (per Busch's 2023 slides: 'ISO/IEC 20059 is based on the Morphing Attack Potential (MAP)'), is defined through successful verification of both contributing subjects. A blend with a single contributing subject has no second subject to verify, so the attack measure does not apply to it.
findings.source: Ferrara, Franco, Maltoni, Busch, Morphing Attack Potential, IWBF 2022, arXiv:2204.13374. https://arxiv.org/pdf/2204.13374 ; and C. Busch, Morphing Attack Detection, slides dated 2023-06-06, https://www.christoph-busch.de/files/Busch-MAD-230606.pdf
findings.quote: a manipulated face image, generated by merging samples of two or multiple subjects in the image domain, might be verified successfully against probe images captured from the contributing subjects.
findings.bears_on: Q2: under the standard's own attack measure a same-subject or mirror self-morph has zero attack potential in the multi-identity sense; the literature does not say whether it is therefore 'not a morph' or 'a harmless morph'. Q1: not addressed.

findings.claim: At the Frontex 2019 conference on morphing the exact Q1 worry was raised from the floor: could a photo 'improved' for genuine reasons be read as a morphing issue. The recorded answers do not give a class label: the moderator (J. Atick) said a beautified image should perhaps be rejected at enrolment, and C. Busch said any manipulation is a problem. In a later session a panellist said test data did include algorithmically beautified photos but the effect was inconclusive. In the same proceedings M. Ferrara's working definition of morphing is purely process-based and does not mention two subjects.
findings.source: Frontex, International Conference on Biometrics for Borders: Morphing and Morphing Attack Detection Methods, Conference Proceedings, Warsaw, 9-10 October 2019, Thematic Sessions 1 and 2 (session summaries, not verbatim transcripts; legal notice says content is not Frontex's official opinion). https://www.statewatch.org/media/2154/eu-frontex-proceedings-conference-biometrics-borders-morphing.pdf
findings.quote: Professor Busch said any manipulation of the image was a problem – whatever its cause. [...] “morphing is a special effect that transforms an image into another through seamless transition”
findings.bears_on: Q1: the question is known to the community but unresolved; the practitioner answer is 'reject or detect all manipulation', which cuts against simply calling such images bona fide, while not calling them morphs either. Q2: Ferrara's working definition is the one process-based definition found, which is compatible with 'method used means morph'; it was given as a talk introduction, not as a standard.
