findings.claim: The SOTAMD and iMARS consortia paper in the Frontex proceedings separates 'morphed' from 'manipulated otherwise' (for example looking younger or more beautiful), and announces that iMARS will categorise admissible image processing versus manipulative processing in order to separate correct bona fide from manipulated images. No published iMARS taxonomy resolving one-photo reconstructions or same-subject morphs was found.
findings.source: Busch, Caillebotte, Seidel, Knopjes, Maltoni, Ferrara, Veldhuis, Spreeuwers, Raja, Raghavendra, Gomez-Barrero, Rathgeb, Face Morphing Attacks: What needs do be done, in Frontex Conference Proceedings 2019. https://www.christoph-busch.de/files/Busch-iMARS-Frontex-2019.pdf
findings.quote: a photograph that has been morphed or manipulated otherwise (e.g. data subjects that want to look younger or more beautiful) [...] iMARS will also categorize and consider admissible image processing steps in contrast to typical manipulative processing steps
findings.bears_on: Q1: European project framing has three groups (bona fide with admissible processing, manipulated otherwise, morphed), which supports not equating single-subject manipulation with morphing; it does not say such images count as bona fide for scoring a morph detector. Q2: silent.

findings.claim: The German Federal Government's bill that introduced digital-only passport photos defines morphing as merging several face images into one that unites the features of two or more faces, and states explicitly that image editing is inadmissible even when it is not morphing, except changes made only to meet format or biometric requirements.
findings.source: Deutscher Bundestag, Drucksache 19/21986, Gesetzentwurf der Bundesregierung: Entwurf eines Gesetzes zur Stärkung der Sicherheit im Pass-, Ausweis- und ausländerrechtlichen Dokumentenwesen (2020), sections A.1 and justification of the PassG amendment. https://dserver.bundestag.de/btd/19/219/1921986.pdf
findings.quote: Eine Bearbeitung des Lichtbilds durch Bildbearbeitungsprogramme ist auch dann unzulässig, wenn sie kein „Morphing“ darstellt. Davon unberührt bleibt eine Veränderung des Lichtbilds, welche allein dazu dient, technische Vorgaben zum Format oder zur Biometrie einzuhalten.
findings.bears_on: Q1 and Q2: a legislator recognises 'editing that is not morphing' as its own class: not a morph, yet not an acceptable photo. Supports separating the tasks; does not support treating reconstructed or self-blended images as clean bona fide. Morph itself is defined by two or more faces.

findings.claim: European project pages define the morphing attack through multiple subjects and describe bona fide as a trusted capture: SOTAMD speaks of samples of multiple subjects merged so that each contributor verifies against one artificial identity, and of a bona fide image 'captured in a trusted environment'; the CORDIS article on iMARS says morphed images normally combine features from different faces. Neither page mentions beautification, synthetic faces or same-subject morphs.
findings.source: SOTAMD project page, https://www.christoph-busch.de/projects-sotamd.html ; CORDIS, Combating identity fraud at Europe's borders (iMARS, grant 883356), https://cordis.europa.eu/article/id/457716-combating-identity-fraud-at-europe-s-borders (both read through a summarising fetch that returned these short quotations)
findings.quote: biometric samples of multiple subjects are merged, in order to allow an unlawful but successful verification [...] These images normally combine features from different faces, creating a composite image.
findings.bears_on: Q2: multi-subject definitions; silent on same-subject morphs. Q1: silent.

findings.claim: Key authors of the standard gloss the bona fide class as 'pristine' or 'genuine' images. This gloss is informal (slides and papers), and the normative ISO/IEC 20059 definition of the bona fide sample could not be read. The ISO/IEC 30107-3 metric definitions shown on the same slides speak of 'bona fide presentations', a term about subject behaviour at a capture device, which NIST replaced by 'bona fide sample' (BSCER) to follow ISO/IEC FDIS 20059.
findings.source: C. Busch, Face Image Morphing keynote slides, 2022-10-11, https://christoph-busch.de/files/Busch-MAD-keynote-221011.pdf ; Tapia, Russo, Busch, Generating Automatically Print/Scan Textures for Morphing Attack Detection Applications, arXiv:2408.09558 ; Scherhag et al. in Frontex Proceedings 2019 ('bona fide (i.e., genuine)') ; NIST report changelog entry of June 6, 2025
findings.quote: It is quantified as the proportion of morphed images that are erroneously verified as bona fide (i.e. pristine) with all contributing subjects. [...] samples of the class bona fide (i.e. a pristine image)
findings.bears_on: Q1: if bona fide means pristine, a GAN or diffusion reconstruction is not strictly bona fide either; it falls in a gap between the two standard classes. This cuts against simply labelling reconstructions bona fide, while still not making them morphs. Q2: a self-morph is likewise not pristine.

findings.claim: From memory, not opened this session: ISO/IEC 30107-3 defines a bona fide presentation as an interaction of the capture subject with the capture subsystem in the fashion intended by the policy of the biometric system, and ISO/IEC 39794-5 carries a 'post acquisition processing' data block that records processing history of a face image. The 39794-5 table of contents entry (clause 7.38 Post acquisition processing block) appeared in a search snippet only; its enumerated values were not seen.
findings.source: ISO/IEC 30107-3 (2017, revised 2023) and ISO/IEC 39794-5:2019; search snippets and memory only
findings.bears_on: Q1: possible lead. A policy-based definition of bona fide would make the answer depend on the issuing authority's policy on processing (which ICAO sets narrowly). Needs verification before citing.

not_found: The normative terms of ISO/IEC 20059:2025 beyond 3.1 (morph, morphing attack, bona fide sample, contributing subject, MACER, BSCER), its clause 5 'Morphing attacks' (the announced definition of biometric sample modifications and manipulation) and clause 7. The ISO Online Browsing Platform and iso.org returned HTTP 403; the VDE, DIN, EVS, GSO and iTeh previews show only front matter, scope and term 3.1. A free copy of ISO/IEC WD 20059 advertised on Busch's 2023 slides sits behind a LinkedIn short link and was not opened. So it is not verified whether the standard's taxonomy says anything about single-subject modifications or same-subject morphs.

Any statement in ISO, NIST, ICAO, Frontex, SOTAMD or iMARS material that a single-subject synthetic face, a GAN-inversion or diffusion-autoencoder reconstruction, or an AI-enhanced photo is a bona fide sample for morph detection, or is an attack for morph detection. None found.

Any statement in those bodies' material on a morph of two images of the same subject, a mirror self-morph or a self-blend. None found. The terms 'self-morph', 'same subject morph' do not occur in the NIST FATE MORPH report, NISTIR 8292, NIST IR 8584, the FATE MORPH API, ICAO Doc 9303 Parts 2, 3 and 9, or the ICAO Portrait Quality report.

A published iMARS deliverable with the announced taxonomy of admissible versus manipulative image processing. Only the 2019 statement of intent was found. A University of Bologna paper (ManipulationDetection_Full_V4.pdf on cris.unibo.it) that reportedly treats beautification, geometric distortion and morphing as separate classes next to non-manipulated bona fide images could not be opened (HTTP 403); known from a search snippet only.
The verbatim ISO/IEC 2382-37 and ISO/IEC 30107-3 definition of 'bona fide presentation', and the enumerated values of the ISO/IEC 39794-5 post-acquisition processing block. Not opened.

An official Frontex or eu-LISA definition of morphing (the Frontex proceedings carry a disclaimer that they are not Frontex's official opinion). The text of recital 32 of Regulation (EU) 2019/1157 on live enrolment was seen only as quoted in secondary slides, not on EUR-Lex.
Whether a newer edition of ICAO Doc 9303 than the Eighth (2021) exists as of November 2026. Not verified; the Eighth Edition files are what icao.int serves today.
stance_summary:
Scope of this sweep: standards and evaluation bodies only (ISO/IEC 20059 and 30107, NIST FATE MORPH, ICAO Doc 9303 and the ICAO portrait report, FVC-onGoing, SOTAMD, iMARS, Frontex, and one national legislator). Seventeen sources were opened and quoted; one item is from memory and marked not checked.

What the bodies agree on. Every definition of morphing that could be read is a multi-subject definition: ICAO ('two or more subjects' faces'), NIST (same wording; 'All morphs are created with two subjects'), ISO/IEC 20059 Introduction and ISO/IEC 30107-1 ('manipulated to match two or more biometric data subjects'; 'multiple identity attack'), FVC-onGoing ('mixing faces of two subjects'), Scherhag et al. 2017 ('at least two subjects'), the German bill ('zweier oder mehrerer Gesichter'). The attack measures (MMPMR, MAP) require both contributing subjects to verify. The negative class is called bona fide, glossed by NIST as 'nonmorph' and by Busch and co-authors as 'pristine' or 'genuine'. In practice the bona fide data of NIST and of the European benchmarks are real photographs of one person, sometimes processed (ICAO-compliance software, cropping, resizing, print and scan).

Q1 (one-photo reconstructions, synthetic single-identity faces, enhanced photos). No standard or evaluation body takes a position. NIST's bona fide sets contain only live captures and print-scanned copies; the words synthetic, retouch and beautification do not appear in its report. What does exist points two ways. (a) In favour of the author's separation: morphing and other manipulation are consistently named as different things (ICAO report: 'photo manipulation and morphing'; SOTAMD and iMARS consortia: 'morphed or manipulated otherwise'; German bill: editing is inadmissible 'even when it is not morphing'; ISO keeps morphing out of the PAD series and lists synthetic patterns under PAD artefacts). NIST also counts flagged print-scanned genuine photos as false detections, the nearest precedent for 'processed single-subject image equals bona fide'. (b) Against simply calling such images bona fide: ICAO Doc 9303 Part 3 forbids any digital alteration that changes appearance, the ICAO portrait report allows only a short closed list of processing steps, the bona fide class is glossed as 'pristine', and at the Frontex 2019 conference the direct question whether a beautified photo could be taken for a morphing issue got the answer that any manipulation is a problem and should be rejected or detected. So the standards support 'this is not a morph and belongs to a different task', but they do not support 'this is a legitimate bona fide'. The image type falls in a gap between the two classes that evaluation standards define. The paper can truthfully say the standards are silent and that the binary bona fide versus morph protocol leaves a third category (single-subject manipulated or generated image) undefined.

Q2 (same-person morphs, mirror self-morphs, self-blends). No standard or evaluation body addresses the case; no test set contains it. The author's position ('if the morphing method is used, it is a morph') is not what the definitions say on a literal reading: they define a morph by the presence of two or more subjects and the attack by a multiple identity outcome, so a one-subject blend is not a morph and has no attack potential under MAP. Two readable sources go further in that direction: the NIST demorphing specification says a bona fide input should return two images essentially identical to the input, and the SOTAMD paper states the demorphing assumption that a genuine image is 'a combination of two identical images (Im = Ia + Ia)'. On the other side, the only process-based definition found is Ferrara's working definition at the Frontex conference ('a special effect that transforms an image into another through seamless transition'), and FVC-onGoing speaks of 'the result of a morphing process', though it immediately adds 'mixing faces of two subjects'. A self-morph is also not a clean bona fide: it is a digitally altered portrait under ICAO rules. Net: the standards neither label a same-subject morph as attack nor as bona fide; by their wording it is outside the attack definition, and by their portrait rules it is outside the compliant bona fide. Who labels it which way in research papers was not part of this sweep (the local notes point to Pimenta et al., arXiv 2309.00549, labelling two-photo 'selfmorphs' genuine; not re-verified here).

Silence and limits. The decisive text, clauses 3, 5 and 7 of ISO/IEC 20059:2025, is paywalled and was not read; its scope announces 'a definition of biometric sample modifications and manipulation', so it may contain a taxonomy relevant to both questions. This should be checked in the purchased standard before the paper claims that ISO has no position. Everything else supports the statement that the field has no explicit stand on either question and that the paper's class definitions need to be stated and argued, not cited.

findings.claim: MorDeephy creates 'selfmorphs' by applying face morphing to two images of the same identity (about 500k from VGGFace2) and labels them BONA FIDE for S-MAD training. Stated reason: automatic landmark morphs carry visible artefacts, so without this the detector learns artefacts; selfmorphs carry the artefacts but keep the identity, so the detector is pushed toward 'deep face features'. Their ablation says selfmorphs matter for generalisation. The paper credits the selfmorph idea to Borghi et al.
findings.source: Medvedev, Shadmand, Goncalves, 'MorDeephy: Face Morphing Detection Via Fused Classification', ICPRAM 2023 (pp. 193-204 per the MorphGuard reference list), arXiv 2208.03110. Full text read via arXiv PDF.
findings.quote: In the proposed method schematic (Fig. 1) we consider selfmorphs as bona fide samples.
findings.bears_on: Q2, against the author's lean: the only MAD group that explicitly reasons about two-photo same-person morphs labels them bona fide, on the ground that identity is retained.

findings.claim: Same label and same reason in the S-MAD alignment study: selfmorphs made with LDM (diffusion) and StyleGAN from images of one individual are treated as bona fide. Note the authors still call them 'morphed images'; the bona fide label is a deliberate design choice, not a claim that no morphing happened.
findings.source: Pimenta, Medvedev, Goncalves, 'Impact of Image Context for Single Deep Learning Face Morphing Attack Detection', arXiv 2309.00549 (PDF read). Venue BIOSIG 2023, DOI 10.1109/BIOSIG58226.2023.10345999, taken from a search snippet of the Coimbra group page, not opened.
findings.quote: Selfmorphs are generated using images of the same individual, resulting in morphed images that continue to represent that same individual but contain merging artifacts of a different kind.
findings.bears_on: Q2, against the author's lean (label bona fide). Also shows the label is applied to generator-based (diffusion, GAN) same-person morphs, not only landmark ones.

findings.claim: The differential (D-MAD) follow-up keeps the rule: landmark and StyleGAN selfmorphs (about 250k each) are counted on the bona fide side and the paper says the dataset is 'balanced by the amount of bona fides and morphs' with selfmorphs in the bona fide half.
findings.source: Medvedev, Pimenta, Goncalves, 'Fused Classification For Differential Face Morphing Detection', arXiv 2309.00665 (PDF read). Venue WACV 2024 Workshops from a search snippet only, not verified on the arXiv page.
findings.quote: We follow the original S-MAD approach [21] and use selfmorphs as bona fide samples to focus on the behavior of deep face features rather than detecting artifacts.
findings.bears_on: Q2, against the author's lean; shows the bona fide label is a stable position of this group across S-MAD and D-MAD.

findings.claim: The same position is repeated in 2025: selfmorphs ('morphed images generated from two different instances of the same identity') made with a landmark method, StyleGAN and a Diffusion Autoencoder are treated as bona fide. The paper cites only Borghi et al. and MorDeephy as prior uses; it does not cite SelfMAD or Kashiani et al., which label one-identity morphs the opposite way.
findings.source: Medvedev, Goncalves, 'MorphGuard: Morph Specific Margin Loss for Enhancing Robustness to Face Morphing Attacks', arXiv 2505.10497v1 (15 May 2025), PDF read. No venue listed on arXiv.
findings.quote: selfmorphs are treated as bona fide samples, ensuring a more balanced training process.
findings.bears_on: Q2, against the author's lean. Evidence that the bona fide convention is current, and that the conflict with other papers is not discussed.

findings.claim: Kashiani et al. do the OPPOSITE with the same construction. Their 'Self-morphing (SM) augmentation' morphs different instances of one identity (StyleGAN, OpenCV, FaceMorpher) and uses the result as a MORPH ATTACK sample (Figure 1: bona fide in green boxes, self-morphed images in red). Stated reason: a same-identity morph has minimal visible artefacts, so it imitates hard, high-quality morphs 'synthesized by two look-alike subjects'. So the attack label is justified as a proxy for artefact-light two-person morphs, not by an argument that a same-person morph is itself a threat.
findings.source: Kashiani, Alipour Talemi, Saadabadi, Nasrabadi, 'Towards Generalizable Morph Attack Detection with Consistency Regularization', IJCB 2023 (per arXiv comments), arXiv 2308.10392. PDF read.
findings.quote: To promote the effectiveness of morph attack images, different instances of the same identity are employed in our morphing attacks.
findings.bears_on: Q2, for the author's lean (method used, so labelled morph attack). Directly contradicts the Coimbra labelling of the same object.

findings.claim: SelfMAD labels a ONE-IMAGE blend as an attack. A bona fide image is blended with a geometrically transformed (translate, elastic, scale) copy of itself, optionally plus synthetic frequency patterns; these get label 1 ('simulated morphing attacks'). A copy that only had colour, brightness, downscale or sharpen changes keeps label 0 ('still considered bona fide'). The paper says the blend is meant to replicate morphing of two different faces and that training is done 'without using actual face morphs'. So the label is a surrogate for the real attack class; the paper does not argue that a self-blend is an attack in its own right. A 2026 tutorial by the first author describes the output as 'synthetic morphs' simulated 'from bona fide images'.
findings.source: Ivanovska, Todorov, Damer, Jain, Peer, Struc, 'SelfMAD: Enhancing Generalization and Robustness in Morphing Attack Detection via Self-Supervised Learning', FG 2025 (per arXiv comments), arXiv 2504.05504. PDF read. Tutorial: Ivanovska, IJCB 2026 tutorial slides 'When Two Faces Become One', lmi.fe.uni-lj.si (text layer read).
findings.quote: y is the corresponding image label, which equals 0 for bona fide images IOS and IAS and 1 for simulated morphing attacks IMS, and IFMS (subscripts flattened by text extraction)
findings.bears_on: Q2, for the author's lean in practice (one-image blend = attack class), but as a training proxy. Also Q1-adjacent: SelfMAD draws its own line, global photometric or quality processing of one photo stays bona fide.

findings.claim: Self-Blended Images, the deepfake method SelfMAD builds on, labels a blend of one pristine image with a transformed copy of itself as FAKE. Reason given: such samples reproduce common forgery traces (blending boundary, statistical mismatch) and are harder, so the classifier generalises; detectors can then be trained 'without forged face images'.
findings.source: Shiohara, Yamasaki, 'Detecting Deepfakes with Self-Blended Images', CVPR 2022 (pages 18720-18729 per the SelfMAD reference list), arXiv 2204.08376. PDF read.
findings.quote: a fake image is generated by blending pseudo source and target images from a single image
findings.bears_on: Q2 by analogy (deepfake field): one-image blend labelled fake, as a proxy. Not a morphing paper.

findings.claim: Face X-ray defines the positive class by PROCESS, not identity: an image is 'manipulated' if it can be decomposed into a blend of two images from different sources, and the training positives are composites of real images only.
findings.source: Li, Bao, Zhang, Yang, Chen, Wen, Guo, 'Face X-ray for More General Face Forgery Detection', arXiv 1912.13458v2 (PDF read). Venue CVPR 2020 from memory, not verified this session.
findings.quote: blended images that are composited from only real ones
findings.bears_on: Q2 by analogy: precedent for a process-based class definition ('blending was applied') in face forgery detection.

findings.claim: The University of Bologna group builds same-subject morphs as an artefact resource, with no attack or bona fide label. Their FRGCS set is morphs of two faces of the same subject with perturbed landmarks to increase artefacts, so each morph has a clean reference image for training and scoring artefact retouching (cGAN in 2021, CodeFormer in 2024). MorDeephy and MorphGuard both name Borghi et al. 2021 as the origin of the selfmorph idea.
findings.source: Di Domenico, Borghi, Franco, Maltoni, 'Face Restoration for Morphed Images Retouching', IWBF 2024, presentation slides at guidoborghi.altervista.org/Academic/iwbf_presentation.pdf (text read). Underlying paper: Borghi, Franco, Graffieti, Maltoni, 'Automated Artifact Retouching in Morphed Images With Attention Maps', IEEE Access 9:136561-136579, 2021; its full text could NOT be opened (repository returned 403), so its content is taken from the slides and from MorDeephy's description.
findings.quote: Morphed images obtained using two faces from the same subject
findings.bears_on: Q2, neutral: a third use of same-subject morphs (image-quality ground truth) that sidesteps the class question. Note they still call them 'morphed images'.

findings.claim: In a human morph detection study, same-person morphs are counted as MORPHS in the single-image 'morph or not' task and as SAME PERSON in the identity task. The data set has 54 different-individual pairs and 54 same-individual pairs (two photos of one person taken at different times), each with a midway morph. In Experiment 2a (one image shown, answer 'morph or not') the morphed-face trials are 27 different-people morphs plus 27 same-person morphs. In Experiment 1a (is the original and the morph the same person) the same-individual morph pairs are the 'same' trials.
findings.source: Nightingale, Agarwal, Farid, 'Perceptual and computational detection of face morphing', Journal of Vision 21(3):4, 2021. Author-hosted PDF farid.berkeley.edu/downloads/publications/jov21.pdf read.
findings.quote: For the morphed face trials, each participant saw 27 different-people midway morphs [...] and 27 same-person midway morphs
findings.bears_on: Q2, for the author's lean on the question 'is this image a morph' (process label), while showing that the identity question gets the opposite answer. The clearest published case of the two-axis treatment.

findings.claim: A face-matching study deliberately uses same-identity morphs as the genuine ('same identity') condition so that the experiment measures identity discrimination and not morph-artefact detection. Same-identity pairs are one unedited image plus a 50/50 morph of two other images of the same person. The paper calls these images 'face morphs' but their ground truth is 'same identity'.
findings.source: Mallick, Jeckeln, Parde, Castillo, O'Toole, 'The Influence of the Other-Race Effect on Susceptibility to Face Morphing Attacks', arXiv 2204.12591 (2022). PDF read. No journal reference on arXiv.
findings.quote: This ensured also that the performance observed in the morph condition was derived from people’s ability to distinguish same- and different-identity pairs, rather than morphed and non-morphed images.
findings.bears_on: Q2, mixed: named a morph (process), scored as genuine (identity). Independent of the Coimbra group, same logic: same-person morphs are the control that separates identity mixing from processing traces.

findings.claim: The 2019 reference survey defines a morph by its effect on identity (it resembles two or more individuals and verifies against all contributors) and uses 'bona fide' as a synonym for 'non-morphed'. The two criteria coincide for ordinary data; the survey never considers a morph whose inputs are one person. It also fixes the term 'mated morph comparison' as a morph compared with an independent sample of one contributing subject, so 'mated morph' does not mean a same-subject morph.
findings.source: Scherhag, Rathgeb, Merkle, Breithaupt, Busch, 'Face Recognition Systems Under Morphing Attacks: A Survey', IEEE Access 7:23012-23026, 2019. Author-hosted PDF dasec.h-da.de/wp-content/uploads/2019/02/morphdet_survey.pdf read.
findings.quote: artificial biometric samples, which resemble the biometric information of two (or more) individuals in image and feature domain
findings.bears_on: Q2: definition ties the morph to two or more contributing subjects; silent on same-subject morphs. By the identity criterion a same-subject morph is not a morphing attack; by the 'non-morphed = bona fide' wording it is not bona fide either.

findings.claim: The 2021 survey likewise speaks of 'contributing subjects' (K = 2 in its formulas) and a morph succeeding only 'if all contributing subjects are verified successfully'. It lists morphing of identical twins and look-alikes as an open problem. It has no mention of same-subject or self morphs.
findings.source: Venkatesh, Ramachandra, Raja, Busch, 'Face Morphing Attack Generation & Detection: A Comprehensive Survey', arXiv 2011.02045 (PDF read); published in IEEE Transactions on Technology and Society 2021 per search snippet.
findings.quote: in the context of biometrics, two or multiple facial images can be combined to resemble the contributing subjects
findings.bears_on: Q2: two-or-more-subjects definition; silence on same-subject morphs.

findings.claim: NIST defines morphing by plurality of people and equates bona fide with non-morph. FATE MORPH (NISTIR 8292): morphing is where 'two or more subjects' faces are morphed or blended together'. NIST IR 8584 (August 2025): 'Morphing methods combine photos of two or more individuals' and uses 'bona fide (non-morph)'. Neither document mentions morphs made from one person, and I found no NIST data set described as containing them.
findings.source: Ngan, Grother, Hanaoka, Kuo, NISTIR 8292 FATE MORPH report (pages.nist.gov/frvt/reports/morph/frvt_morph_report.pdf) and NIST IR 8584 'FATE MORPH 4B: Considerations for Implementing Morph Detection in Operations' (nvlpubs.nist.gov/nistpubs/ir/2025/NIST.IR.8584.pdf). Both text layers searched. Author list from memory.
findings.quote: Face morphing is an image manipulation technique where two or more human faces are blended or merged into a single photograph.
findings.bears_on: Q2: definition by two or more individuals; silence on same-subject morphs. Q1: 'bona fide' means 'non-morph', nothing about generated or reconstructed single-identity images.

findings.claim: The ISO standard frames the threat as a 'multiple identity attack': morphing attacks are those 'where biometric references are manipulated to match two or more biometric data subjects', and the scope promises a definition of sample modifications 'with a specific focus on manipulations that constitute a multiple identity attack'. Under that framing a same-subject morph is a sample manipulation but not a multiple identity attack. I could read only the introduction, scope and term 3.1 (free preview); the normative definitions of morph, morphing attack and bona fide are behind the paywall and the ISO Online Browsing Platform returned 403.
findings.source: ISO/IEC 20059:2025, 'Information technology - Methodologies to evaluate the resistance of biometric systems to morphing attacks', first edition 2025-08. Official preview PDF from VDE Verlag (assets.vde-verlag.de/iec-normen/preview-pdf/info_isoiec20059%7Bed1.0%7Den.pdf) read.
findings.quote: morphing attacks, where biometric references are manipulated to match two or more biometric data subjects submitted during enrolment
findings.bears_on: Q2: the standard's attack concept is identity multiplicity, which does not cover a same-subject morph. Exact term definitions not verified.

findings.claim: The 2022 open-access handbook repeats the plural-identity definition in its introduction and in the MAD evaluation chapter. A text search of the whole book found no passage on morphs of one subject or self-morphs.
findings.source: Rathgeb, Tolosana, Vera-Rodriguez, Busch (eds.), 'Handbook of Digital Face Manipulation and Detection', Springer 2022, open access at library.oapen.org (handle 20.500.12657/52835). Chapter 1 and the chapter by Spreeuwers, Schils, Veldhuis, Kelly. Full text searched.
findings.quote: Face morphing is a technique to combine facial images of two (or more) subjects such that the result resembles both subjects.
findings.bears_on: Q2: two-or-more-subjects definition; silence on same-subject morphs.

findings.claim: In SynMorph, 'mated samples' are NOT same-subject morphs. They are extra non-morph images of the same synthetic identity, made by editing identity-irrelevant attributes of a StyleGAN2 base sample in latent space and filtered by a face recogniser; they sit in the non-morph subset and serve as D-MAD references. Base samples are forced to be distinct identities (VGGFace2 cosine-distance threshold 0.45), and morphs are made only between different base samples.
findings.source: Zhang, Ramachandra, Raja, Busch, 'SynMorph: Generating Synthetic Face Morphing Dataset with Mated Samples', arXiv 2409.05595. PDF read.
findings.quote: corresponding mated samples are generated by applying different attribute editing techniques to the original base sample
findings.bears_on: Q2: by design same-identity material goes to the bona fide side and morphs are only cross-identity. Q1: one-identity GAN latent edits (no second identity) are used as bona fide in a morphing data set.

findings.claim: SMDD assigns the attack label purely by process. Morph pairs are drawn at random from StyleGAN2-ADA samples; in the pairing passage I found no check that the two parents are different identities or that the morph succeeds against a face recogniser.
findings.source: Damer, Lopez, Fang, Spiller, Pham, Boutros, 'Privacy-friendly Synthetic Data for the Development of Face Morphing Attack Detectors', CVPR Workshops 2022, arXiv 2203.06691. Pairing section read; author list and venue from memory.
findings.quote: The morphing pairs are selected randomly to allow for a larger variety of similarities between the pairs.
findings.bears_on: Q2, weakly for the author's lean: a standard training set labels by 'the morphing tool was applied', not by verified identity mixing. Q1: its bona fide class is fully synthetic single-identity images.

findings.claim: Demorphing and identity-disentanglement papers define the morph by identity count: a morph 'comprises two identities' and a non-morph is the degenerate case where the decomposition returns the input. Shukla and Ross open with a hedged definition ('usually pertaining to two distinct identities') and report that for a non-morph the method 'merely replicates the input'. Under this view a same-subject morph behaves as a non-morph.
findings.source: Banerjee, Ross, 'Conditional Identity Disentanglement for Differential Face Morph Detection', IJCB 2021, arXiv 2107.02162; Shukla, Ross, 'Facial Demorphing via Identity Preserving Image Decomposition', IJCB 2024, arXiv 2408.10993. Both PDFs read.
findings.quote: A face morph is created by combining the face images usually pertaining to two distinct identities.
findings.bears_on: Q2, against the author's lean implicitly: identity-count definition, same-identity input would be treated as non-morph. No explicit statement about same-subject morphs.

findings.claim: Two 2026 D-MAD papers take the identity view explicitly. Jin et al. analyse the bona fide case as a morph of two samples of one identity and argue it stays in that identity's cluster. Kelly et al. define a morph as a mix of 'different persons' and argue that D-MAD and face recognition do essentially the same task.
findings.source: Jin, Nishigaki, Ohki, 'Face Re-morphing: Differential Morphing Attack Detection via Feature-Space Similarity Changes', arXiv 2608.13858 (Aug 2026); Kelly, Spreeuwers, Veldhuis, 'Find the Differences: Differential Morphing Attack Detection vs Face Recognition', arXiv 2604.14734v2 (Apr 2026). Both PDFs read.
findings.quote: the image generated by re-morphing two samples of the same identity is also likely to be recognized as identity I
findings.bears_on: Q2, against the author's lean for D-MAD: under identity-based detection a same-identity morph is, by construction, on the bona fide side. Neither paper discusses labelling policy.

findings.claim: Bologna D-MAD work treats morphs with a weak second identity as attacks all the same and adds artefact analysis because identity features fail there. It states that real morphs are often made 'with a stronger presence of the accomplice' and shows morphs wrongly called bona fide by an identity-only detector 'even though visible artifacts are present'. No lower limit on the second identity's share is given at which a morph stops being a morph.
findings.source: Di Domenico, Borghi, Franco, Maltoni, 'Dealing with Subject Similarity in Differential Morphing Attack Detection', arXiv 2404.07667. PDF read.
findings.quote: the morphed image is often created with a stronger presence of the accomplice
findings.bears_on: Q2, for the author's lean: process traces are accepted as legitimate evidence of a morph when identity evidence is weak. Silent on the limiting case of zero second identity.

findings.claim: The mirror self-morph exists in face perception research, where it is called a 'perfectly symmetric version' of the SAME face, never a different identity. Rhodes et al. made it with commercial morphing software by averaging each face with its mirror image, and noted that such blends have blend side effects (more average, smoother skin). They also cite Langlois et al. 1994, who blended forward and mirror images of 16 shots of one face and called the result 'same-face composites'.
findings.source: Rhodes, Proffitt, Grady, Sumich, 'Facial symmetry and the perception of beauty', Psychonomic Bulletin & Review 5(4):659-669, 1998. PDF copy at homepages.uc.edu read.
findings.quote: Perfectly symmetric versions were created using Gryphon's Morph software to average the normal and mirror images of each face.
findings.bears_on: Q2, mirror case: outside biometrics the object is a processed image of one person made with a morphing tool. No security labelling. I found no MAD paper that builds or labels a photo-plus-mirror morph.

findings.claim: Two further non-MAD precedents treat same-person blends as legitimate representations of a person. (a) Within-person 'face averages' are built by morphing about 30 photos of one person to a common shape and averaging; they are proposed as a better stored reference for automatic face recognition. (b) Face frontalisation fills poorly visible pixels with the mean of the pixel and its mirror-symmetric counterpart ('soft symmetry') as preprocessing of genuine probes.
findings.source: (a) Robertson, Kramer, Burton, 'Face Averages Enhance User Recognition for Smartphone Security', PLOS ONE 2015, doi 10.1371/journal.pone.0119460, page text read. (b) Hassner, Harel, Paz, Enbar, 'Effective Face Frontalization in Unconstrained Images', arXiv 1411.7964, PDF read; venue CVPR 2015 and author list from memory.
findings.quote: Each celebrity’s average texture was then morphed onto their average shape to produce their face average
findings.bears_on: Q2, against the author's lean at the identity level: in face recognition research a same-person morph or mirror blend is a processed genuine sample, even a preferred enrolment image. Tangential to MAD.

findings.claim: The opposing papers do not engage with each other. Full-text searches show: SelfMAD cites neither Medvedev/MorDeephy nor Kashiani; MorphGuard (2025) cites neither SelfMAD nor Kashiani nor Self-Blended Images; Kashiani cites neither MorDeephy nor Borghi nor Self-Blended Images. I found no paper in the MAD literature that poses the question 'is a same-subject or one-image morph an attack or a bona fide' and argues an answer.
findings.source: Own full-text keyword search of arXiv PDFs 2504.05504, 2505.10497 and 2308.10392 this session (names: medvedev, mordeephy, kashiani, selfmad, ivanovska, shiohara, borghi), plus several web searches for explicit discussions.
findings.bears_on: Q2: research has no explicit, argued stand. Two opposite labelling conventions coexist unacknowledged, each justified by the training goal of the paper that uses it.

findings.claim: One deepfake preprint does take the explicit position that self-blends are NOT fakes: it calls Self-Blended Images a 'non-generative manipulation', calls detector hits on them 'false positives', and reports that adding self-blends to the real class lowers cross-dataset AUROC (89.3 to 82.8 in its Table 2 text). The paper was WITHDRAWN on 4 Nov 2026 because training reals overlapped with test sets, so its numbers should not be relied on.
findings.source: Yermakov, Cech, Fritz, Matas, 'The Alpha Blending Hypothesis: Compositing Shortcut in Deepfake Detection', arXiv 2605.10334 v1 (11 May 2026), withdrawn in v2. Abstract page and v1 PDF read.
findings.quote: yielding false positives on this non-generative manipulation
findings.bears_on: Q2 by analogy and Q1: the closest explicit statement that a one-image blend belongs on the genuine side and that flagging it is a false alarm. Deepfake field, withdrawn preprint, low weight.

findings.claim: Incidental Q1 evidence from an S-MAD paper: bona fide images are passed through the GAN (reconstructed, no second image) and kept as BONA FIDE, on purpose, so the detector learns morphing patterns and not general GAN patterns.
findings.source: Zhang, Ramachandra, Raja, Busch, 'Generalized Single-Image-Based Morphing Attack Detection Using Deep Representations from Vision Transformer', arXiv 2501.09817v1 (Jan 2025). PDF read.
findings.quote: reconstructed bona fide images are applied to the datasets with GAN-based morphing algorithms
findings.bears_on: Q1, for the author's lean: a leading MAD group labels one-photo GAN reconstructions bona fide and treats 'general patterns from GANs' as something a morph detector should not key on.

not_found: No MAD paper was found that builds a morph from one photo and its own mirror image, or that uses facial symmetry or a flip-consistency score as a morph cue. The mirror self-morph appears only in face perception research (Rhodes et al. 1998) as a 'symmetric version' of the same face.

No paper was found that explicitly asks and argues whether a same-subject morph or a one-image self-morph is an attack or a bona fide. The papers that create such images each state a label and a training motive, and do not cite the papers that label the opposite way.

No benchmark or public test set (NIST FATE MORPH, FRLL-Morphs, SMDD, SynMorph, SYN-MAD 2022, MorDeephy protocols) was found to contain same-subject morphs in either class at test time, and no paper was found that reports detector error on same-subject morphs as a diagnostic. This was not checked exhaustively for every data set.

ISO/IEC 20059:2025 normative terms (morph, morphing attack, bona fide, contributing subject) could not be read: the free preview stops at term 3.1 and the ISO Online Browsing Platform and iso.org returned HTTP 403. Only the Introduction and Scope wording is verified.

Borghi, Franco, Graffieti, Maltoni, IEEE Access 2021 (the cited origin of selfmorphs) could not be opened: cris.unibo.it, iris.unimore.it and core.ac.uk returned 403 or a Cloudflare challenge. One attempt to fetch it with a browser user-agent string was blocked by the permission system and not retried. Its use of same-subject morphs is reported second-hand from the group's IWBF 2024 slides and from MorDeephy and MorphGuard.

SelfMAD++ (Information Fusion, ScienceDirect S1566253525009832) and IDSwapMAD (EURASIP Journal on Information Security 2026, doi 10.1186/s13635-026-00227-9) were seen only as search results; both pages refused the fetch. Their labelling is not verified.

Kraetzer et al., IH&MMSec 2017 (media forensics model of legitimate editing versus morphing) and the ICAO Portrait Quality technical report (rule against digitally altered portraits) were not opened; both bear more on Q1 than Q2.

The term 'mated' does not denote same-subject morphs anywhere I looked: 'mated morph comparison' (Scherhag et al.) is a morph against a sample of one contributor, and SynMorph 'mated samples' are non-morph images of the same identity.

Published venues not verified on a primary page: Pimenta et al. as BIOSIG 2023 and Medvedev et al. 2309.00665 as WACV 2024 Workshops (search snippets only); Face X-ray as CVPR 2020, SMDD as CVPR Workshops 2022 and Hassner et al. as CVPR 2015 (memory).
stance_summary:
Q2 (same-person morphs, one-image self-morphs). The literature has no agreed and no argued stand. What exists is three layers that do not meet.

(1) Definitions. Every definition I could open ties a morph or a morphing attack to two or more people: Scherhag et al. 2019, Venkatesh et al. 2021, NIST FATE MORPH and NIST IR 8584, the 2022 Springer handbook, and the introduction of ISO/IEC 20059:2025, which names the threat a 'multiple identity attack'. The same sources use 'bona fide' to mean 'non-morphed'. For ordinary data these two criteria (identity mixing, and the morphing process having been applied) always agree, and none of these sources considers the case where they split. Read literally, a same-subject morph is not a morphing attack (one identity) and is not bona fide either (it is morphed). The ISO term definitions themselves were not readable.

(2) Papers that actually make such images label them by their training goal, in opposite directions. Bona fide: the Coimbra group in four papers 2022 to 2025 (MorDeephy, Pimenta et al., the D-MAD paper, MorphGuard), for two-photo same-person morphs made with landmark, GAN and diffusion methods, with the stated reason that identity is kept and the detector should not learn artefacts. Attack: Kashiani et al. (IJCB 2023), for the same two-photo same-person construction, as a stand-in for artefact-light look-alike morphs; SelfMAD (FG 2025) and its deepfake parent Self-Blended Images (CVPR 2022), for one-image blends, as a surrogate for real attacks. Neither attack-side paper claims a one-identity morph is a threat in itself. Unlabelled: the Bologna group uses same-subject morphs only as artefact carriers with a clean reference. These camps do not cite each other.

(3) Outside MAD training. Nightingale, Agarwal and Farid (Journal of Vision 2021) is the clearest precedent for the author's position: in the single-image 'morph or not' task, same-person morphs are counted as morphs, while in the identity task the same images are 'same person'. Mallick et al. 2022 use same-identity morphs as the genuine control precisely to separate identity from morph traces. Identity-based D-MAD and demorphing work (Banerjee and Ross, Shukla and Ross, Jin et al., Kelly et al.) implicitly put a one-identity image on the non-morph side. Face perception and face recognition research treat a mirror blend or a within-person average as a processed image of the same person. No MAD paper on a mirror self-morph was found.

So the author's Q2 lean ('if the morphing method is used, it is a morph') has real precedent (Kashiani, SelfMAD, Nightingale Experiment 2a, process-based class definitions such as Face X-ray, by-process labelling in SMDD), but it runs against the only MAD group that explicitly reasons about same-person morphs and against the identity-multiplicity wording of the standard threat model. The sources support separating two words that the field uses interchangeably: 'morph' (a process was applied) and 'morphing attack' (a multiple-identity threat). A paper can state which one its positive class means, cite both conventions, and say truthfully that the question has not been discussed.

Q1 (one-photo reconstructions). This sweep was not aimed at Q1 and is mostly silent on it. Incidental findings, all on the author's side: Zhang et al. 2025 keep GAN-reconstructed bona fide images in the bona fide class so that the detector does not learn general GAN patterns; SynMorph places GAN-edited single-identity 'mated samples' in the non-morph subset; SMDD uses fully synthetic single-identity faces as bona fide; SelfMAD keeps photometrically processed copies bona fide; one withdrawn deepfake preprint calls detector hits on self-blends false positives. NIST and the surveys define bona fide only as 'non-morph' and say nothing about generated or reconstructed single-identity images.

Process notes. All work was read-only; PDFs were streamed and searched in memory. One WebFetch call saved a copy of a PDF on its own to /home/narolski/.claude/projects/-home-narolski-mambamorph/c2840dc9-dd37-4619-9347-d8a76080b93f/tool-results/webfetch-1794406551304-pwwbej.pdf; that was the tool's behaviour, not a deliberate write. Quotes were copied from extracted PDF text, so line-break hyphens and subscripts may differ slightly from the typeset originals.

findings.claim: The Darmstadt/Twente/Bologna/NIST methodology paper states that bona fide and morphed samples must have equal quality, because otherwise texture classifiers may separate the classes by compression or quality differences and not by morphing. It names rescaling, image optimisation and rotation as further post-processing that can leave such nuisance artefacts.
findings.source: Scherhag, Nautsch, Rathgeb, Gomez-Barrero, Veldhuis, Spreeuwers, Schils, Maltoni, Grother, Marcel, Breithaupt, Raghavendra, Busch, "Biometric Systems under Morphing Attacks: Assessment of Morphing Techniques and Vulnerability Reporting", BIOSIG 2017. https://www.christoph-busch.de/files/Scherhag-Methodology-BIOSIG-2017.pdf
findings.quote: for morphing detection, it is important to obtain an equal quality for bona fide and morphed samples, in order to avoid bias towards different quality levels on the morphing detection algorithm. [...] might classify the images according to such compression artefacts or image quality differences, if present, instead of attributes related to the morphing process. The same applies for other artefacts introduced by some post-processing, e.g. rescaling, image-optimization or rotation.
findings.bears_on: Both, indirectly. Establishes that resize, compression, rotation and similar processing are treated as nuisance that must not separate the classes. The phrase "attributes related to the morphing process" frames the detection target as the process, which is mildly in line with the author's Q2 lean, but the paper says nothing on same-person morphs or on one-photo reconstructions.

findings.claim: The NIST IFPC 2018 slide deck from the same group lists "Consistent quality of the database (bona fides vs morphs)" as a major factor and says a classifier is otherwise biased towards quality levels. It illustrates this with BRISQUE scores of a bona fide (21.0), an uncompressed morph (29.1) and a compressed morph (50.0).
findings.source: Gomez-Barrero, Scherhag, Nautsch, Rathgeb, Veldhuis, Spreeuwers, Schils, Maltoni, Grother, Marcel, Breithaupt, Raghavendra, Busch, "Vulnerability Evaluation for Presentation + Morphing Attacks", slides, NIST IFPC, 28 Nov 2018. https://www.christoph-busch.de/files/Gomez-NIST-IFPC-Vulnerability-181128.pdf
findings.quote: Equal quality for bona fide and morphed samples is important. Otherwise, the classifier is biased towards different quality levels
findings.bears_on: Q1 indirectly (processing history must not define the class). Silent on Q2 and on generative processing.

findings.claim: The Darmstadt FERET/FRGCv2 MAD database applies every post-processing variant to both classes: unprocessed, resized to 360x480, JPEG2000 to 15 KB, and print-scan followed by JPEG2000 to 15 KB. The paper says reference images of both classes should undergo realistic post-processing and criticises earlier datasets as unrealistic when they lack print-scan. It also states that no lossy compression was applied before post-processing.
findings.source: Scherhag, Rathgeb, Merkle, Busch, "Deep Face Representations for Differential Morphing Attack Detection", arXiv:2001.01202v2 (preprint of the IEEE TIFS 2020 paper).
findings.quote: To reflect this variety, the passport images (bona fide and morphed) of the MAD database are post-processed in different manners. [...] the reference images (bona fide and morphed) should have undergone various realistic post-processings including strong JPG2000 compression and print-scan transformation.
findings.bears_on: Q1 indirectly: resize, JPEG2000 at ICAO file size and print-scan are treated as normal history of a bona fide passport image. Silent on Q2 and on generative processing.

findings.claim: The Scherhag et al. survey treats post-processing mainly as something an attacker does to hide a morph (sharpening, histogram equalisation, blurring) plus the unavoidable print and scan, and notes that ICAO storage at 15 to 20 kB may make double-compression detection infeasible. It asks for public print-scan databases of bona fide and morphed images. It does not state an explicit rule that bona fide images must receive the same processing.
findings.source: Scherhag, Rathgeb, Merkle, Breithaupt, Busch, "Face Recognition Systems Under Morphing Attacks: A Survey", IEEE Access 2019. Author copy: https://dasec.h-da.de/wp-content/uploads/2019/02/morphdet_survey.pdf
findings.quote: publicly available large-scale databases of printed and scanned bona fide and morphed face images are required
findings.bears_on: Q1 indirectly (print-scan and ICAO compression are part of a genuine image's life). Silent on Q2 and on generative processing.

findings.claim: In the SOTAMD benchmark the bona fide enrolment images were cropped and resized to follow the inter-eye distance distribution of the morphs so that image size cannot reveal the class. Bona fide enrolment images were also printed and scanned, and all enrolment images of both classes passed ICAO compliance software. One submitted algorithm converted all training images to PNG to avoid JPEG artefacts being detected.
findings.source: Raja, Ferrara, Franco, Spreeuwers, Batskos, de Wit, Gomez-Barrero, Scherhag, Fischer, Venkatesh, Singh, Li, Bergeron, Isadskiy, Ramachandra, Rathgeb, Frings, Seidel, Knopjes, Veldhuis, Maltoni, Busch, "Morphing Attack Detection - Database, Evaluation Platform and Benchmarking", arXiv:2006.06458v3 (IEEE TIFS 2021).
findings.quote: The bona fide enrolment images have been cropped to remove the background and resized in order to follow the same inter-eye distance distribution of the morphed images, so that it's not possible to infer the image class from its size.
findings.bears_on: Q1 indirectly: explicit equalisation of resize and print-scan between classes in the main European benchmark. Silent on Q2 and on generative processing.

findings.claim: Spreeuwers et al. name double JPEG compression as a cue that reflects one way of building morphs and not morphing itself, and tell dataset builders to store morphs losslessly. In their experiments Gaussian noise and down-up scaling are applied to the morphed images only, as a disguise, and raise within-dataset EER from below 5% to above 20% (noise) and above 12% (scaling). This is not an equalisation experiment: bona fide images are not given the same noise or scaling.
findings.source: Spreeuwers, Schils, Veldhuis, "Towards Robust Evaluation of Face Morphing Detection", EUSIPCO 2018, https://new.eurasip.org/Proceedings/Eusipco/Eusipco2018/papers/1570439319.pdf ; and Spreeuwers, Schils, Veldhuis, Kelly, "Practical Evaluation of Face Morphing Attack Detection Methods", chapter 16 of the Handbook of Digital Face Manipulation and Detection, Springer 2022 (open access copy at library.oapen.org).
findings.quote: When creating morphed face images, it is vital to save them in a lossless format like '.png' to ensure the morphing detection methods do not detect compression artifacts. [...] Such a method will fail to detect morphed images if they are stored uncompressed.
findings.bears_on: Q1 indirectly (compression history is a shortcut, not the attack). Silent on Q2 and on generative processing.

findings.claim: The Magdeburg group put legitimately edited genuine photos into the genuine (negative) class when training a morph detector, and defined that legitimate editing as in-plane rotation, scaling and cropping. They also recompressed all training and test images to JPEG quality 100 so that compression history is the same for both classes. They warn that legitimate image processing can produce feature distributions similar to morphs.
findings.source: Makrushin, Neubert, Dittmann, "Automatic Generation and Detection of Visually Faultless Facial Morphs", VISAPP 2017. https://www.scitepress.org/PublishedPapers/2017/61311/61311.pdf
findings.quote: the second one encompasses original images as well as images after legitimate editing usually performed by photographers. This includes in-plane rotation, scaling and cropping.
findings.bears_on: Q1: the clearest research statement found that a processed genuine photo stays in the genuine class, but only for geometric edits. Nothing on generative or one-image blends. Silent on Q2.

findings.claim: Seibold et al. apply the same noise and blur to both genuine and morphed training images so that the network cannot use low-level statistics created by the morphing pipeline.
findings.source: Seibold, Samek, Hilsmann, Eisert, "Accurate and Robust Neural Networks for Security Related Applications Exampled by Face Morphing Attacks", arXiv:1806.04265.
findings.quote: we apply some kinds of noise and blur to change this distributions in the original and forged face images to prevent the network from discriminating on these characteristics and to focus on more semantic high-level models.
findings.bears_on: Q1 indirectly (equalising low-level history across classes is an established practice). Silent on Q2.

findings.claim: In the NTNU line, the three standard data media are digital, print-scan, and print-scan with compression, and both morphs and bona fide images are printed, scanned and compressed to at most 15 KB to mimic passport application and chip storage.
findings.source: Zhang, Ramachandra, Raja, Busch, "Generalized Single-Image-Based Morphing Attack Detection Using Deep Representations from Vision Transformer", arXiv:2501.09817 (CVPRW 2024). Passages returned by the fetch tool from the arXiv HTML page.
findings.quote: Both generated morphs and bona fide images are printed using DNP-DS820 dye-sublimation photo printer [...] Print-scanned images (morphs and bona fide) are compressed into less or equal to 15 KBs
findings.bears_on: Q1 indirectly (print-scan and compression are benign history applied to both classes). Silent on Q2.

findings.claim: NIST FATE MORPH computes one of its false detection rates (BSCERq) on the source images of each morph set in order to keep quality consistent between bona fides and morphs. NIST defines morphing by the number of subjects. NIST also reports that many differential detectors, at developer thresholds, classify most printed and scanned photos as morphs even when they are not.
findings.source: Ngan, Grother, Hanaoka, Kuo, "FATE MORPH Part 4: Performance of Automated Face Morph Detection", NISTIR 8292 draft supplement, version dated 14 September 2026. Read from the local copy /tmp/claude-1000/-home-narolski-mambamorph/c2840dc9-dd37-4619-9347-d8a76080b93f/scratchpad/research_repo/research/synid/papers/2026_ngan_face-analysis-technology-evaluation-fate-part-4.pdf (public page: https://pages.nist.gov/frvt/html/frvt_morph.html).
findings.quote: This method attempts to maintain consistent quality between the bona fides and morphs within in each dataset. [...] Face morphing is an image manipulation technique where two or more subjects' faces are morphed or blended together to form a single face in a photograph. [...] many differential morph detectors, at a developer-defined threshold, show low morph miss rates BUT very high false detection rates, which means the algorithms are classifying most scanned photos as morphs, even when they're not.
findings.bears_on: Q1: direct evidence that a benign operation (print and scan) on genuine photos causes false alarms, and that NIST counts these as errors. Q2: the NIST definition is by subject count (two or more subjects), which a same-person or mirror self-morph does not meet; NIST does not discuss that case.

findings.claim: Counter-example to equalisation inside the same research line: in the PRNU morph detection paper, histogram equalisation, scaling and sharpening are applied to the morphed images only, framed as attacker post-processing. Bona fide images are left unprocessed.
findings.source: Debiasi, Scherhag, Rathgeb, Uhl, Busch, "PRNU-based Detection of Morphed Face Images", IWBF 2018. https://www.christoph-busch.de/files/Debiasi-PRNUMorphDetection-IWBF-2018.pdf
findings.quote: different techniques, which aim at further modifying the quality of the morphed face images
findings.bears_on: Q1 indirectly: shows the field uses two framings of post-processing (attacker concealment applied to morphs only, versus document pipeline applied to both), so equalisation is advised but not uniformly practised. Silent on Q2.

findings.claim: Ferrara, Franco and Maltoni show that networks trained only on digital images fail on printed and scanned images of both classes; they add simulated print-scan images of both classes to training. In their score convention higher means bona fide, so a score near 0 for a print-scanned bona fide is a false alarm (my reading of the convention from the following sentences of the paper).
findings.source: Ferrara, Franco, Maltoni, "Face morphing detection in the presence of printing/scanning and heterogeneous image sources", arXiv:1901.08811 (IET Biometrics).
findings.quote: the networks trained on digital images only [...] return a score close to 0 for both bona fide and morphed images. This means that the modifications introduced by P&S remove the textural details that makes bona fide and morphed images distinguishable.
findings.bears_on: Q1: benign processing of a genuine photo moves detector scores to the morph side; treated as a robustness failure of the detector. Silent on Q2.

findings.claim: The Darmstadt handbook chapter defines the bona fide reference class as an unaltered passport image. It reports that, with training on original images, JPEG2000 compression and print-scan raise the D-EER of the best single-image detector (HOG) while deep-feature differential detection stays robust.
findings.source: Scherhag, Rathgeb, Busch, "Face Morphing Attack Detection Methods", chapter 15 of the Handbook of Digital Face Manipulation and Detection, Springer 2022 (open access, library.oapen.org/bitstream/20.500.12657/52835/1/978-3-030-87664-7.pdf).
findings.quote: The bona fide reference images correspond to an unaltered passport image and should meet the corresponding quality criteria.
findings.bears_on: Q1: the word "unaltered" in the definition of bona fide cuts against calling a generative reconstruction a plain bona fide, although the same authors apply resize, JPEG2000 and print-scan to their bona fide images. Q2: silent.

findings.claim: The only study found that measures false alarms of morph detectors on beautified genuine images: a skin-smoothing filter applied to AMSL (FRLL-based) test images raised BPCER at the original threshold from 25.2% to 70 to 80% for AlexNet and from 18.1% to 90 to 100% for VGG19, and EER from 27.6% and 19.0% to about 41% and 37 to 43%. The authors keep the filtered genuine images labelled bona fide, call the filter an unmalicious alteration and call the errors false rejections. Limits: two CNNs, one dataset, one simple filter, arXiv preprint.
findings.source: Concas, La Cava, Panzino, Orru, Masala, Marcialis, "Deceptive Beauty: Evaluating the Impact of Beauty Filters on Deepfake and Morphing Attack Detection", arXiv:2509.14120v1, September 2025 (venue not verified).
findings.quote: VGG19 suffers a complete collapse in the detection of bona fide images after even minimal filtering [...] even innocent beautification practices by bona fide users can inadvertently resemble adversarial manipulations, leading to increased false rejections
findings.bears_on: Q1: closest analogue to the author's position. A processed genuine photo is kept in the bona fide class and flagging it is counted as a false alarm. It concerns a classical smoothing filter, not a generative reconstruction. Q2: silent.

findings.claim: The NTNU/Darmstadt survey lists face beautification as an open issue whose impact on MAD had not been investigated, while expecting that passport photos are beautified before application in many countries.
findings.source: Venkatesh, Ramachandra, Raja, Busch, "Face Morphing Attack Generation & Detection: A Comprehensive Survey", arXiv:2011.02045 (IEEE Transactions on Technology and Society, 2021).
findings.quote: Another aspect that was not investigated yet with its impact on MAD is potential face beautification. It is expected that the face images are beautified prior to applying for the passport in many countries [96]. As the beautification process changes the image properties, it is essential to understand both vulnerability and MAD for this particular problem.
findings.bears_on: Q1: explicit statement of a gap. The field acknowledged in 2021 that it had no position on beautified genuine photos in MAD. Q2: silent.

findings.claim: A Darmstadt workshop paper notes that applicants can edit, including beautify, the photo before submission, finds that morphs score as more beautiful (smoother) than bona fide images, and ends by raising, not answering, the question of how beautified images affect morph detection.
findings.source: Tapia, Ibsen, Busch, "Beauty Score Fusion for Morphing Attack Detection", BMVC 2024 workshop (SRBS). https://bmva-archive.org.uk/bmvc/2024/workshops/SRBS/0006.pdf
findings.quote: various types of image editing, including facial beautification, can be performed prior to the submission of the facial image to the administration [...] Our finding raised the question of the impact of beautifying images and their effects on evading morph detection.
findings.bears_on: Q1: implies smoothing is a cue shared by morphs and beautified genuine photos, and leaves the labelling question open. Q2: silent.

findings.claim: In the Darmstadt retouching line, retouching detection is a separate task with its own detector. There the positive (reject) class is the retouched image and bona fide means unaltered. JPEG at 20 kB and JPEG2000 at 15 kB are applied to both bona fide and retouched reference images.
findings.source: Rathgeb, Bernardo, Haryanto, Busch, "Effects of Image Compression on Face Image Manipulation Detection: A Case Study on Facial Retouching", arXiv:2103.03654 (IET Biometrics 2021).
findings.quote: machine learning-based classifiers are trained to distinguish between bona fide (unaltered) and retouched face images
findings.bears_on: Q1: supports treating non-morph manipulations of one genuine photo as a different detection task from MAD, with its own label set. In that task the altered genuine photo is not bona fide. This is consistent with "do not confuse the tasks" but not with "it is simply a bona fide". Q2: silent.

findings.claim: The ICAO portrait report gives a closed list of processing allowed between capture and the portrait: in-plane rotation, cropping, down-sampling, white balance adjustment, ICC colour management transformation, one RAW conversion, and compression (JPEG ratio not above 15:1; lossy compression at most once per step by camera, photographer or citizen, and issuer). It forbids local modification of the face and background removal by the applicant, and discourages sharpening to boost MTF. It names photo manipulation and morphing as risks of homemade portraits and puts morphing prevention out of its scope. It predates generative tools and does not mention them.
findings.source: ICAO Technical Report "Portrait Quality (Reference Facial Images for MRTD)", Version 1.0, April 2018, clauses 4.4, 7.3, 9.4, 9.5. https://www.icao.int/sites/default/files/TRIP/Publications/TR-Portrait-Quality-v1.0.pdf
findings.quote: No other post processing than In-plane rotation and/or Cropping and/or Down sampling and/or White balance adjustment and/or ICC colour management transformation and/or Processing RAW images into the target encoding (once) and/or Compression as described in Clause 9.5. shall be applied on the captured image to create the portrait. [...] The face images shall not be modified locally, e.g., for removal of scars, pimples or other skin impurities or to modify the shape or location of the nose, the eyes, the eyebrows or any other facial landmarks. (bullet marks removed)
findings.bears_on: Q1 and Q2: the best sourced statement of what an issuing authority regards as benign. A GAN or diffusion reconstruction, an AI enhancement, a mirror self-morph or a same-person morph is none of the listed operations, so none is an acceptable unaltered portrait under this report. The report does not say whether such an image is a morph.

findings.claim: ICAO Doc 9303 requires that the displayed facial image is a true likeness and is not digitally altered or enhanced to change the subject's appearance.
findings.source: ICAO Doc 9303, Machine Readable Travel Documents, Eighth Edition 2021, Part 3, section 3.9.1. https://www.icao.int/sites/default/files/publications/DocSeries/9303_p3_cons_en.pdf
findings.quote: not be digitally altered or enhanced to change the subject's appearance in any way.
findings.bears_on: Q1 and Q2: the rule is tied to change of appearance, not to the tool used. It gives no MAD class label.

findings.claim: National rules read this session ban any software alteration of the submitted photo, and Canada names AI tools explicitly and counts technical corrections and enhancements as alteration. The UK requires the digital photo to be unaltered by computer software.
findings.source: Government of Canada (IRCC), passport photo requirements, https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/canadian-passports/photos.html ; UK government, https://www.gov.uk/photos-for-passports (both read through the fetch tool, which returned the quoted sentences).
findings.quote: be an original photo that isn't altered or edited in any way [...] This includes photo editing software, filters, and AI tools. (Canada) ; unaltered by computer software (UK)
findings.bears_on: Q1: issuing authorities do address generative or AI enhancement of a genuine photo, and they reject it at intake. That is an acceptance rule for documents, not a statement that a morph detector should flag such images.

findings.claim: The US Department of State passport photo page is reported to tell applicants not to change the photo using computer software, phone apps or filters, or artificial intelligence. I could not open the page (HTTP 403), so the wording comes from a search result only.
findings.source: US Department of State, travel.state.gov passport photo pages (for example https://travel.state.gov/content/travel/en/passports/how-apply/photos.html).
findings.bears_on: Q1: same direction as the Canadian rule, not verified.

findings.claim: NIST's operational guidance defines morphing as blending two or more human faces, says a flagged photo is either a morph or a legitimate photo (a false detection), recommends attended live enrolment or other trusted capture as the main prevention, and notes that morphs may be touched up or printed and scanned. It does not discuss retouched, beautified or AI-enhanced genuine photos as a source of false detections.
findings.source: Ngan, Grother, "FATE MORPH 4B: Considerations for Implementing Morph Detection in Operations", NIST IR 8584, August 2025. https://nvlpubs.nist.gov/nistpubs/ir/2025/NIST.IR.8584.pdf
findings.quote: Face morphing is an image manipulation technique where two or more human faces are blended or merged into a single photograph. [...] An investigation, if successful, will reveal that this flagged photo is a morph or a legitimate photo i.e., a false detection.
findings.bears_on: Q1: NIST has a two-way split (morph or legitimate photo) and is silent on a third category of altered genuine photos. Q2: definition requires two or more faces; same-person and one-image self-morphs are not discussed.

findings.claim: Live enrolment is presented by the research community as the strongest countermeasure and is in use in some countries, which removes applicant-side editing altogether. Busch's 2022 slides list Norway and Sweden as live enrolment countries and Finland as moving to signed studio photos, cite EU Regulation 2019/1157 recital 32, and describe bona fide as pristine. Ferrara and Franco call live enrolment the most effective solution but unlikely to be adopted everywhere. Germany accepts only digital photos from 1 May 2025, and Fraunhofer IGD claims its detector separates harmless image editing from security-relevant tampering without defining harmless.
findings.source: Busch, "Face Image Morphing" keynote slides, 11 Oct 2022, https://christoph-busch.de/files/Busch-MAD-keynote-221011.pdf ; chapter by M. Ferrara and A. Franco in the Handbook of Digital Face Manipulation and Detection, Springer 2022 (chapter title not verified) ; Fraunhofer IGD news item, 1 May 2025, https://www.igd.fraunhofer.de/en/media-center/news-from-the-institute/2025/legal-amendment-on-biometric-passport-photos-effective-may-1-2025.html. The EUR-Lex text of the regulation itself was not opened.
findings.quote: Switching to live enrolment would certainly be the most effective solution, but its adoption by all the involved countries is very unlikely (Ferrara and Franco) ; It can distinguish between harmless image editing and security-relevant tampering (Fraunhofer IGD) ; erroneously verified as bona fide (i.e. pristine) (Busch slides)
findings.bears_on: Q1: the practical ideal of a bona fide is a live or trusted capture with only issuer-side processing. Where that holds, generative enhancement by the applicant cannot occur. No class label is given for edited genuine photos. Q2: silent.

findings.claim: The AMSL dataset page says its genuine images (from the Face Research Lab London set) were modified to comply with the ICAO portrait quality standard and to fit on an eMRTD chip, that is, the genuine class of this widely used benchmark is already a processed image.
findings.source: AMSL Face Morph Image Data Set, licence and description page, Otto-von-Guericke University Magdeburg. https://omen.cs.uni-magdeburg.de/disclaimer/index.php (read through the fetch tool).
findings.quote: modified in the way to comply with the requirements of the ICAO portrait quality standard for eMRTD
findings.bears_on: Q1 indirectly: benchmark practice already accepts resize and compression as bona fide history. The page did not state the exact resize and JPEG settings. Silent on Q2.

One targeted search for morph detector false alarms on restored or super-resolved genuine photos returned nothing relevant.

They are leads, not evidence.

A statement in any MAD paper that bona fide and morphs must share the same processing as an explicit protocol rule, beyond the BIOSIG 2017 and NIST IFPC 2018 advice on equal quality, was not found. Practice varies (see Debiasi et al. 2018 and Spreeuwers et al. 2018, where processing is applied to morphs only).
stance_summary:
What this literature settles. There is a clear, sourced position that processing history must not separate the classes. Since 2017 the Darmstadt, Twente, Bologna and NIST authors have said that bona fide and morphed samples need equal quality, or the classifier learns compression and quality (BIOSIG 2017; NIST IFPC 2018 slides). Reference datasets then applied the same resize, JPEG or JPEG2000 to about 15 kB, and print and scan to both classes (Scherhag et al. 2020; SOTAMD; the NTNU print-scan protocols), and NIST keeps a quality-matched false detection rate (BSCERq). Practice is not uniform: several papers apply sharpening, histogram equalisation, noise or rescaling to morphs only, as attacker concealment.

Which operations count as benign for a bona fide. Research practice: crop, in-plane rotation, resize, JPEG and JPEG2000 at ICAO file sizes, print and scan, and ICAO compliance normalisation. Makrushin et al. (2017) explicitly place photos after "legitimate editing usually performed by photographers" (rotation, scaling, cropping) in the genuine class. The authority view is narrower and explicit: ICAO's Portrait Quality report (2018, clause 9.4) allows only rotation, cropping, down-sampling, white balance, ICC colour transformation, one RAW conversion and limited compression, and forbids local modification of the face. Doc 9303 forbids digital alteration or enhancement that changes appearance. Canada and the UK reject any software alteration, and Canada names AI tools. Live enrolment (Norway, Sweden, and Germany's digital-only rule from May 2025) is the stated ideal.

Q1 (one-photo reconstructions, enhanced or beautified genuine photos). The MAD literature in this area has no stated position on generative reconstruction of a single genuine photo. I found no paper that tests it or labels it. The nearest evidence points in two directions. (a) Benign processing of genuine photos does cause false alarms and these are counted as detector errors: NIST reports detectors calling most scanned photos morphs; Ferrara et al. show the same for print and scan; Concas et al. (2025, preprint) show BPCER rising to 70 to 100% after a smoothing filter and call this an innocent, unmalicious alteration leading to false rejections. That supports the author's view that a morph detector should not be penalised, or should be measured separately, on non-morph alterations. (b) The same community defines bona fide as unaltered or pristine (Scherhag et al. 2022; Busch slides; Rathgeb et al. 2021), treats retouching detection as its own task in which the altered genuine photo is the reject class, and issuing authorities do not accept edited or AI-processed photos. So the sources support "a different task", but they do not support calling a generative reconstruction an ordinary bona fide. Venkatesh et al. (2021) and Tapia et al. (2024) state openly that the effect of beautification on MAD is an unanswered question. Synthetic single-identity bona fides (SMDD) were outside this search topic.

Q2 (same-person morphs, mirror self-morphs, self-blends). This body is silent. No source opened here discusses or labels such images. Every definition opened is by identity count: two or more subjects or faces blended into one image (NIST IR 8584, NIST FATE MORPH, BIOSIG 2017, Fraunhofer IGD). Read literally, a one-person self-morph does not meet those definitions, which goes against the author's "if the method is used, it is a morph". One sentence in BIOSIG 2017 says detectors should rely on "attributes related to the morphing process", which is process-based wording and could be cited for the author's view, but it was written about compression shortcuts, not about this case. Under the ICAO rules a self-morph is a locally modified image and so not an acceptable portrait, whatever its class label.

Bottom line for the paper. On equalising processing there is a stand, and it can be cited. On Q1 and Q2 the literature covered here has no stand: the labels are implied by convention (bona fide means unaltered; morph means two or more subjects) and the two conventions leave one-photo generative reconstructions and one-person self-morphs unassigned. The paper can state that and must define its own classes. ISO/IEC 20059 and 39794-5 definitions were not accessible and should be checked before the claim of silence is made final.
