corrected_stance_summary:
Scope of my check: I re-opened 24 of the searcher's items this session (arXiv HTML, CVF, Springer, NIST PDF, BMVC PDF, the ISO publisher preview, Crossref). Every quotation I could reach is exact. Corrections are to venues, to the count of Coimbra papers, and to two statements about what the literature lacks. I could not open Borghi et al. 2021 (HTTP 403 everywhere), the ISO term entries beyond 3.1, or SelfMAD++.

Q2 (same-person morphs, one-image self-morphs, the mirror self-morph). The searcher's picture needs one substantive correction: the literature is not merely silent with one group against the author. It is openly split in labelling practice, and nobody has stated a definition.

1. Same-person, two-photo morph labelled BONA FIDE: one group (Coimbra) in five papers, 2022 to 2025 (MorDeephy, ICPRAM 2023; Pimenta et al., BIOSIG 2023; Fused Classification for differential detection, arXiv 2309.00665; Quadruplet Loss, IWBF 2024; MorphGuard, arXiv 2505.10497). Their reason: the identity is unchanged, and the detector should not learn tool artefacts. They still call these images "morphed images". Their own evidence of benefit is mixed (MorDeephy calls selfmorphs important; the IWBF 2024 paper says they "didn't demonstrate significant impact").

2. Same-person, two-photo morph labelled ATTACK: Kashiani et al., IJCB 2023 (missed by the searcher). They run StyleGAN, OpenCV and FaceMorpher on two instances of one identity and call the results "morph attacks", to get morphs with few visible artefacts. This is the same object as in point 1 with the opposite label. It is the nearest published precedent for the author's reading ("if the morphing method is used, it is a morph"), but it is a training augmentation, not a stated definition.

3. One-image self-blend labelled ATTACK: SelfMAD (FG 2025) states label 1 for its simulated morphs, built by blending an image with a transformed copy of itself, as a stand-in for "the image-level morphing of two non-identical faces". It inherits this from self-blended images in deepfake detection (Shiohara and Yamasaki, CVPR 2022).

4. Definitions point the other way from the author's reading, by wording only. NIST ("two or more subjects' faces"), ISO/IEC 20059:2025 (scope: "manipulations that constitute a multiple identity attack"; introduction: references "manipulated to match two or more biometric data subjects"), the Venkatesh et al. survey (the attack "breaks the rule of single ownership"), the NTNU and Idiap introductions, and Kashiani's own introduction all define the attack by two or more people and by its effect on the identity link. Under that wording a same-person morph or a mirror self-morph is not a morphing attack, because only one person can verify against it. None of these sources discusses the case.

5. Mirror self-morph: I found no morphing attack detection source that uses or labels one. Outside the field it is an old, standard single-identity manipulation (Rhodes et al. 1998: "Perfectly symmetric versions, made by blending the normal and mirror images of each face").

So for the paper: academia has no stated stand on whether a same-person or mirror self-morph is a morph. There are two opposed labelling practices for the two-photo case (one group each way), one attack-side practice for one-image blends as a surrogate, and standards wording that defines the attack by multiple identities and would therefore place a mirror self-morph outside the attack class. The author's reading has a precedent (Kashiani et al.; SelfMAD) but is not the consensus and conflicts with the effect-based wording of NIST and ISO. Whichever label the paper adopts, it should say that it is a choice between a process-based and an identity-based definition, cite both practices, and note that the mirror variant appears to be new in this field. The claim "this is undiscussed and worth discussing" is supported.

Q1 (one-photo reconstructions, synthetic single-identity faces, enhanced photos). The searcher's summary stands, with these corrections and additions.

- Venue: the NTNU ViT paper is CVPR Workshops 2024 (pp. 1510-1518), not an unpublished January 2025 preprint. It is the earlier statement of the rationale ("learn patterns generated from morphing instead of general patterns from GANs"); SynMorph (IEEE Access 2025) repeats it and adds that the fix is only partial.
- SynMorph's own conclusion uses "bona fide" as the opposite of "synthetic", so even the paper that puts reconstructions in the non-morphed class does not use the term consistently.
- Missed contrast: in generated-image detection the one-image reconstruction of a real photo is the canonical FAKE (Rajan et al., arXiv 2410.11835: "we reconstruct all the real images using the LDMs autoencoder ... The fakes created this way"; Guillaro et al., CVPR 2025: "fake images are generated from real ones"). In morphing attack detection the NTNU papers make the same object the canonical NON-MORPH. The same image gets opposite labels in the two fields. This is the most direct published evidence that they are different tasks, and it supports the author's Q1 position better than anything in the searcher's list. It remains true that no morphing paper says so in words, that Colbois and Marcel argue the opposite for GAN morphs (quotes confirmed, with their hedges "looks like" and "seems to confirm"), and that no paper reports a false alarm rate on reconstructed or enhanced genuine photos.
- NIST and ISO: bona fide means "nonmorph" at NIST; ISO/IEC 20059 frames the attack as a multiple identity attack. Under both, a one-photo reconstruction or a fully synthetic single-identity face is not an attack. Neither tests or discusses such images.

Remaining limits: Borghi et al. 2021 unread, so the origin of "self-morphing" rests on what two citing papers say; ISO term entries for morph and morphing attack unseen; MorphGuard and arXiv 2309.00665 venues not verified; Rajan et al. venue not verified.

corrected_stance_summary:
The standards findings hold up, but the searcher's conclusion needs one important addition: research papers do take explicit positions on same-person morphs, and they take opposite ones.

What I did. I re-opened all 19 sources the searcher marked as checked and saw the quoted text in each. I found two errors of detail. First, the 2026 NIST report does not keep the 2020 print-and-scan sentence: it now says differential detectors over-flag scanned photos, while some single-image detectors show the opposite pattern. Second, the FVC-onGoing S-MAD page itself attributes its metrics to ISO/IEC FDIS 20059, not the DIS. The one item marked not checked is half confirmed: the ISO/IEC 30107-3 definition of bona fide presentation ("in the fashion intended by the policy of the biometric system") was seen in a national terminology database; the ISO/IEC 39794-5 values were not.

Q2, standards. Confirmed: every readable definition (ICAO, NIST, ISO/IEC 20059 Introduction and Scope, ISO/IEC 30107-1, FVC-onGoing, Scherhag et al. 2017, the German bill) defines a morph by two or more subjects. None mentions a same-person morph, a mirror self-morph or a self-blend, and no test set contains one. The standards are silent, and on their literal wording a one-subject blend is outside the attack definition.

Q2, research literature (missed by the searcher, all opened this session). Two camps exist.
- Same-person morph labelled bona fide. Four papers from the Coimbra group apply landmark, StyleGAN and diffusion morphing to two photos of one identity and put the result in the bona fide class: MorDeephy (arXiv:2208.03110), "we consider selfmorphs as bona fide samples"; Medvedev, Pimenta, Gonçalves (arXiv:2309.00665); Pimenta, Medvedev, Gonçalves (arXiv:2309.00549); MorphGuard (arXiv:2505.10497). Their reason: identity is retained, and the detector should learn identity mixing, not blending artefacts.
- One-image self-blend labelled attack. SelfMAD (Ivanovska et al., FG 2025, arXiv:2504.05504) blends a bona fide image with a geometrically transformed copy of itself and labels the result 1, "simulated morphing attacks". It follows Self-Blended Images in deepfake detection (CVPR 2022), where self-blends are the fake class. Their reason: the detector should learn the traces of the process.
In the passages I read, both camps use these images as training data only; nobody evaluates on them, and nobody states a definition. I found no source on a mirror-image self-morph specifically.

So for the author's position ("if the morphing method is used, it is a morph"): it is a process-based definition. It matches SelfMAD's labelling practice, conflicts with the Coimbra group's labelling, and conflicts with the literal wording of every standard definition read. The honest statement for the paper is that standards are silent, the research literature is split by what the detector is meant to detect (identity mixing versus process traces), and no one has argued the choice explicitly.

Q1. Confirmed silence. No standard or evaluation body says whether a one-photo GAN or diffusion reconstruction, a synthetic single-identity face or an AI-enhanced photo is bona fide or attack for a morph detector. The supporting picture is as the searcher described: morphing and other manipulation are named as separate things (ICAO portrait report, the SOTAMD and iMARS consortia paper, the German bill, ISO keeping morphing out of the PAD series), which supports treating generated-image detection as a different task. But ICAO forbids any appearance-changing alteration and allows only a short list of processing steps, so such an image is not a compliant portrait either. Two additions: informal glosses of 'bona fide' split between "pristine/genuine" (Busch, Tapia, Scherhag) and "nonmorph/not attack" (NIST, SMDD), and only the second would cover a reconstruction; and SMDD (arXiv:2203.06691) is a research precedent that uses 50,000 fully synthetic faces as the bona fide class.

Limits. Clauses 3, 5 and 7 of ISO/IEC 20059:2025 remain unread by me as well (ISO browsing platform returned 403); the scope announces "a definition of biometric sample modifications and manipulation", so the purchased standard must be checked before the paper says ISO has no position. The session's web search budget ran out, so my search for missed sources was cut short; in particular I ran no search for mirror-image blends. I wrote no files and did not open the local notes.

Bears on Q2: same-person morph labelled bona fide, because "deep discriminative face features remain after performing selfmorphing".

"We follow the original S-MAD approach [21] and use selfmorphs as bona fide samples to focus on the behavior of deep face features rather than detecting artifacts." Dataset: about 250k landmark-based and 250k GAN-based selfmorphs counted among the bona fides. Q2: bona fide.

Medvedev, Gonçalves, MorphGuard: Morph Specific Margin Loss for Enhancing Robustness to Face Morphing Attacks, arXiv:2505.10497 (opened; venue not verified). "we incorporate selfmorphs — morphed images generated from two different instances of the same identity" and "selfmorphs are treated as bona fide samples"; includes a Diffusion Autoencoder-based morphing method. Also states "The use of selfmorphing is not a novel concept. Borghi et al. [65] previously used it to introduce artificial artifacts". Q2: bona fide.

The pixel-artifact generator "performs pixel space blending of the original source image IOS and the geometrically transformed version of IAS" (translation, elastic transform, scaling of the same image); the label "equals 0 for bona fide images IOS and IAS and 1 for simulated morphing attacks IMS, and IFMS". Q2: a one-image self-blend with a transformed copy is put in the attack class, as a training proxy. This is the opposite labelling to the Coimbra papers.

"SBIs are generated by blending pseudo source and target images from single pristine images" and serve as "fake samples". Q2 by analogy: in the neighbouring deepfake field a one-image self-blend is the fake class. SelfMAD cites it.

Borghi, Franco, Graffieti, Maltoni, Automated Artifact Retouching in Morphed Images with Attention Maps, IEEE Access 2021 (NOT opened: the Bologna repository returned HTTP 403; bibliographic details from a search snippet). Named by MorDeephy and MorphGuard as the origin of self-morphing: used to create images with morphing artefacts whose originals serve as ground truth for a retouching GAN. Should be opened before citing.

Text seen: MAD solutions are trained to differentiate "MAs and bona fide (BF) (i.e. not attack) face images"; dataset of "30,000 attack and 50,000 bona fide samples", "all based on synthetic data". Q1: research precedent for fully synthetic single-identity faces as the bona fide class, and a 'not attack' gloss of bona fide that differs from the 'pristine' gloss.

ISO/IEC 30107-3 term 3.1.2 'bona fide presentation', as reproduced in the Czech terminology database for ČSN ISO/IEC 30107-3, https://www.nlfnorm.cz/terminologicky-slovnik/248392 (opened through a summarising fetch). Definition is policy-based: interaction with the capture subsystem "in the fashion intended by the policy of the biometric system"; the standard also says "the evaluator shall define bona fide presentations and representative test subjects for the target application and population". Q1: under this logic, whether a processed image counts as bona fide depends on the system's policy, which ICAO sets narrowly. Check exact wording in the purchased standard.

NIST 2026 FATE MORPH report, print-and-scan paragraph of the Executive Summary (opened). The wording changed from 2020: it is now differential detectors that classify "most scanned photos as morphs, even when they’re not", while "Some single-image morph detectors show very low false detection rates BUT very high morph miss rates". Anyone quoting NIST on print-scan false alarms for S-MAD must cite the 2020 report, not the current one.

U.S. Department of State passport photo page, https://www.travel.state.gov/en/passports/apply/help/photos.html (NOT opened: HTTP 403; wording seen in a search snippet only). Snippet: "Do not change your photo using computer software, phone apps or filters, or artificial intelligence." Q1 lead: an issuing authority that names AI editing explicitly as inadmissible, without calling it morphing. Must be opened before citing.

CEN/TS 18099:2024 Biometric data injection attack detection (scope read through a summarising fetch of https://www.evs.ee/en/cen-ts-18099-2024). The scope text covers definitions of biometric data injection attacks and injection attack instruments and excludes presentation attack testing; it does not mention synthetic images, deepfakes or morphing. corrected_stance_summary:
Scope of this check. I re-opened 30 or so primary sources and verified every quotation in the findings against the page text. All quotations are exact. Two factual errors and one hedging error were found, and the summary for Q2 needs a material correction. The web-search budget for the session ran out part-way through, so my search for missed sources was short (three queries on self-morphs, one on reconstructed bona fide); ISO/IEC text was not opened.

Errors to fix before anything is cited.
1. Aligned Datasets (arXiv 2410.11835, ICLR 2025) is by Rajan, Ojha, Schloesser and Lee, not "Rajan, Usman, Sud, Lee".
2. Deepfake-Eval-2024: non-AI photoshopped images are in the "Unknown" column of the labelling codebook, not in "Real".
3. AEROBLADE only "suspects" the JPEG/PNG storage bias in DIRE; it does not report it as established.
Venues that were "not verified" are now verified and listed in the checks (Mandelli et al. is WIFS 2024; Cannas et al. is ICCV Workshops 2025; Stay-Positive is ICML 2025; DiFF is ACM MM 2024; SIDA is CVPR 2025; Zhang et al. is CVPR Workshops 2024; Cozzolino et al. is CVPR Workshops 2024; Chai et al. is ECCV 2020; Fake or JPEG is ECCV 2024 Workshops; UniAttackData is IJCAI 2024; AutoGAN is WIFS 2019; Tolosana et al. is Information Fusion 64, 2020).

Q1, one-photo reconstructions. The searcher's summary stands. In generated-image detection the majority practice is that a real image passed through a generator is fake (AutoGAN, Chai et al., DRCT, Aligned Datasets, B-Free, DDA; Stay-Positive states the rule). A smaller set of forensic papers keeps the processed real image in the real class and calls a "synthetic" verdict an error (Cozzolino et al., Cannas et al.), and Mandelli et al. propose a separate "laundered" class. The face-manipulation taxonomies keep morphing apart from entire face synthesis. In MAD, SMDD uses generated faces as bona fide and Zhang et al. use GAN-reconstructed bona fide images, each without arguing a definition. Colbois and Marcel take the opposite line and treat deep-morph detection as synthetic-image detection; a third paper from the same lab (Colbois, Shahreza, Marcel, IJCB 2023, arXiv 2402.00695) again scores morphs with a GAN-image detector against real FFHQ photos. No source says how a morph detector should be scored on a one-photo reconstruction. That gap is real and the paper can name it. I could not test the searcher's claim that no generated-image detection paper trains with reconstructions in the real class.

Q2, same-person morphs and one-image self-morphs. The searcher's "almost silent" is not correct. What the sources show:
- Mirror self-morph (one photo with its own mirror image): no source found, by the searcher or by me. This is "not found in a short search", not "does not exist".
- Two-photo same-person morphs exist in the MAD literature under the name "selfmorphs", and the label is split.
  Bona fide: Medvedev, Shadmand, Gonçalves (MorDeephy, ICPRAM 2023): "we consider selfmorphs as bona fide samples". Pimenta, Medvedev, Gonçalves (BIOSIG 2023): "considering selfmorphs as bona fide samples we can prioritize morphing detection based on the behavior of deep facial features". Medvedev, Pimenta, Gonçalves (WACV Workshops 2024): "use selfmorphs as bona fide samples". All three are one group. Their reason: the image still shows one person, and labelling it bona fide stops the detector from relying on blending artifacts.
  Morph attack: Kashiani, Talemi, Saadabadi, Nasrabadi (IJCB 2023): their Self-morphing augmentation "synthesize morph attacks with minimal visual artifacts using several instances of the same identity". Their reason: same-person morphs stand in for well-made, low-artifact attacks.
  No label: Borghi, Franco, Graffieti, Maltoni (IEEE Access 2021) morph "two images of the same subject" only to simulate artifacts for a retouching network.
- One-image self-blends are in the attack or fake class wherever they appear: SelfMAD (FG 2025) in MAD; SBI (CVPR 2022) and Li and Lyu's face-warping method (CVPR Workshops 2019) in deepfake detection. FaceForensics (2018) calls its same-video self-reenactment output "manipulated (re-rendered) facial imagery".
- Definitions do not settle it. The morph class is defined by identity count: NIST IR 8292, "two or more subjects' faces are morphed or blended together"; the FVC-onGoing S-MAD benchmark, "a morphing process (mixing faces of two subjects)"; Tolosana et al. and the 2022 Handbook, "two or more individuals". The bona fide class is defined as untouched: NIST, "bona fide (nonmorph)"; Borghi et al., "bona fide (not manipulated)". A same-person or one-photo morph fits neither definition as written. No paper I opened argues the point.
- Every use above is a training-time choice. None is an evaluation class, and no benchmark or standard I opened gives a rule.

What the paper can say. There is no agreed stand on same-person or one-image morphs. The author's rule ("if the morphing method is used, it is a morph") has precedent in Kashiani et al., SelfMAD and the deepfake self-blending line, but the most explicit statements inside MAD (the three Coimbra papers) label same-person morphs bona fide, and the standard definitions are written in terms of two or more identities. So the author's rule is a position the paper must state and defend, not a consensus it can cite. Reporting results under both labelings would let readers of either view use them.

Applying this reenactment technique to a video, we obtain video pairs consisting of ground truth data and manipulated (re-rendered) facial imagery." Exploration of Incremental Synthetic Non-Morphed Images for Single Morphing Attack Detection. arXiv 2510.09836 (arXiv comment 'Workshop paper accepted NeurIPS 2025'). OPENED (arXiv HTML). corrected_stance_summary:
Bottom line. After re-opening the sources, the searcher's main conclusion stands: the morphing attack detection literature has no argued position on whether a same-person morph or a one-image self-morph is an attack or a bona fide image, and nobody in that literature has built or labelled a photo morphed with its own mirror image. Three points in the searcher's summary need correcting, and one line of evidence was missing. I could not run fresh keyword searches (the session's search budget ran out after two), so the 'nothing found' statements rest on the searcher's searches plus my full-text checks of the papers.

Q2, what the sources say.

1. Definitions. Scherhag et al. 2019, Venkatesh et al. 2020, NISTIR 8292, NIST IR 8584 and the 2022 Springer handbook all describe a morph as a combination of the faces of two or more people and use bona fide to mean non-morph. None considers a morph with one contributing person. SMDD words it differently: bona fide is "(i.e. not attack)".
   Correction: the ISO/IEC 20059:2025 preview does not say that the attack concept is only identity multiplicity. Its scope reads "morphing attacks, including multiple identity attacks", which makes the multiple identity attack a special case. The term definitions are still unread, so the standard cannot be cited for either side.

2. Papers that make such images label them by training goal, in opposite directions, and do not cite each other (confirmed by full-text search).
   - Bona fide: the Coimbra group in four papers, 2022 to 2025 (MorDeephy, Pimenta et al., the D-MAD paper, MorphGuard). This is a training-only convention; their public benchmark has no selfmorphs in the test data. Even they call the images "morphed images" and write "non-morphed (which are bona fide + selfmorphed)".
   - Attack: Kashiani et al. (IJCB 2023) for two-photo same-person morphs; SelfMAD (FG 2025) for one-image self-blends, which the paper itself calls the "morphed source image", while a photometrically changed copy "is still considered bona fide"; Self-Blended Images (CVPR 2022) in deepfake detection. All three use the label as a stand-in for real attacks, not as a claim that a one-person morph is a threat.
   - Correction: the Bologna group is probably not neutral. Their IWBF 2024 slides show the same-subject set (FRGCS) retouched and tested against an S-MAD model together with ordinary morph sets, with the result described as the model "misclassifies morphed as bona fide", and then used for fine-tuning. That places same-subject morphs on the morphed side. The paper itself returned 403, so this needs one read of the paper before it is cited.
   - Correction: the withdrawn Yermakov et al. preprint does not argue that self-blends are genuine. Its own detector uses them as fakes, and it reports that labelling them real "creates a conflict". It is evidence that this label choice changes what a detector learns.

3. Outside detector training. Nightingale, Agarwal and Farid (Journal of Vision 2021) count same-person morphs as morphs in the single-image "morph or not" task and as the same person in the identity task. Mallick et al. 2022 use same-identity morphs as the genuine control. Identity-based D-MAD and demorphing work (Banerjee and Ross, Shukla and Ross, Jin et al., Kelly et al.) puts a one-identity image on the non-morph side by construction. Face perception research (Rhodes et al. 1998) makes exactly the mirror object with morphing software and calls it a "perfectly symmetric version" of the same face, with "blending artifacts".

4. Missing from the searcher's account: the opposite edge case exists and the field follows identity there. Colbois, Otroshi Shahreza and Marcel (IJCB 2023) generate "morphing attacks" by inverting an averaged face embedding, with no warping or blending of images at all. So when process and identity effect disagree in that direction, the literature calls the image a morph because of its identity effect. This weakens 'the method was used' as the field's criterion, although it says nothing direct about a morphing tool applied to one person.

Answer to the question as asked. In the literature a mirror self-morph is a morphed image in the process sense: every source that builds same-person morphs calls them morphs or morphed images. It is not a morphing attack under any published definition, since all of them require two or more people. Whether an S-MAD evaluation should score it as attack or as bona fide is unsettled: two groups, probably three, put same-person or one-image morphs on the attack side, one group puts them on the bona fide side, and none discusses the other. The author's lean has precedent but is not a consensus. A paper can truthfully write that, to the authors' knowledge, the question has not been discussed, should state which meaning its positive class has (morphing process applied, or multiple-identity attack), and would be safest reporting results under both labellings.

Q1, one-photo reconstructions. Practice in MAD papers supports the author's lean, without any explicit rule: Zhang et al. 2025 keep GAN-reconstructed bona fide images bona fide so the detector does not learn "general patterns from GANs"; SynMorph counts GAN-edited single-identity images as non-morphed; SMDD uses fully synthetic bona fide; IDSwapMAD (2026) uses face-swapped images as the bona fide class for D-MAD. Two things pull the other way and should be acknowledged. Generated-image detection gives the same object the opposite label on purpose (Rajan et al. train a detector to separate real images from their autoencoder reconstructions), which supports 'different task' but shows the label is task-dependent. One-class MAD (Ivanovska and Struc, IWBF 2023) flags anything unlike untouched bona fide images, so such detectors would flag reconstructions by design. NIST says only "bona fide (non-morph)" and "unaltered/non-morphed".

corrected_stance_summary:
Scope of this check. I re-opened 23 of the 24 sources (PDF text extracted and read, or page fetched); the quotations on equal quality, ICAO, NIST, Makrushin, Concas, Venkatesh, Tapia and Rathgeb are accurate. One source stays unopened (US State Department, HTTP 403), as do EUR-Lex recital 32 and the ISO/IEC 20059, 39794-5 and 30107 term entries. The web-search budget for this session was exhausted before I could search, so the hunt for missed sources used leads from the local notes plus direct fetches; absence claims below are limited accordingly.

What stands. The searcher's account of processing equalisation is correct and citable: equal quality for both classes (BIOSIG 2017; IFPC 2018 slides), the same resize, JPEG2000 and print-scan on both classes (Scherhag et al. 2020; SOTAMD; NTNU), NIST's quality-matched BSCERq, and the mixed practice where concealment processing is applied to morphs only (Debiasi 2018; Spreeuwers 2018). The ICAO, Doc 9303, Canada and UK rules are quoted correctly and are intake rules, not class labels.

Main correction, Q2 (same-person morphs, self-blends, mirror self-morph). The searcher's conclusion that the literature is silent is wrong. There is a stand, but it is split, implicit, and confined to training-set design:
(a) Bona fide. The Coimbra group labels two-photo same-person morphs bona fide: MorDeephy (arXiv:2208.03110; ICPRAM 2023 according to the reference list of arXiv:2309.00549) says "we consider selfmorphs as bona fide samples", so that detection rests on "deep face features behaviour, rather than ... detecting artefacts"; repeated for S-MAD (arXiv:2309.00549) and D-MAD (arXiv:2309.00665), including GAN-based selfmorphs. They credit the selfmorph idea to Borghi et al., IEEE Access 2021 (not opened).
(b) Attack. Kashiani et al. (IJCB 2023, arXiv:2308.10392) use same-identity self-morphs as morph attacks in training. SelfMAD (FG 2025, arXiv:2504.05504) labels a one-image self-blend 1, "simulated morphing attacks", following Self-Blended Images (CVPR 2022) from deepfake detection.
(c) Definitions. Every definition opened is by number of individuals and by threat: BIOSIG 2017 ("samples of two or multiple subjects ... to allow a successful verification of all contributing subjects"), NIST IR 8584 and FATE MORPH ("two or more"), the Scherhag survey, Fraunhofer IGD, and ISO/IEC FDIS 19792 as quoted on Busch's MAD page. Read literally, a one-person morph is not a morphing attack. SelfMAD itself defines morphs as blends "of two or more individuals" and uses self-blends only as a proxy.
Consequences for the author's lean ("if the method is used, it is a morph"): it matches the labelling practice in (b), but nobody states it as a definition; it contradicts (a) and the literal definitions in (c). No paper puts same-person morphs or self-blends into a test set with a label, none debates the choice, and none of the sources opened mentions a mirror self-morph. So the paper should not say "the literature is silent"; it should say that two opposite training-label conventions exist without discussion, that formal definitions count subjects, and that the mirror case is unaddressed. That is a real gap worth a paragraph, and the Coimbra papers must be cited as the opposing convention.

Main correction, Q1 (one-photo reconstructions, synthetic and edited genuine photos). Also not silent. Zhang, Ramachandra, Raja and Busch (arXiv:2501.09817) place "reconstructed bona fide images" in the bona fide class of GAN-morph subsets so that the model learns morphing "instead of general patterns from GANs"; this is direct precedent for the author's lean from the NTNU/Darmstadt group. SMDD and SYN-MAD 2022 use fully synthetic StyleGAN2-ADA faces as the bona fide class. SelfMAD states that a colour, sharpness or down-scale augmented image "is still considered bona fide". Against this, generated-image detection labels the same kind of image fake (DRCT, Aligned Datasets, B-Free), which supports treating it as a different task with a different label set. Two working definitions of bona fide coexist: "non-morphed, i.e., bona fide" (Scherhag survey) and "bona fide (nonmorph)" (NIST), versus "unaltered passport image" (handbook ch. 15) and "bona fide (unaltered)" (retouching paper). Under the first, a one-photo reconstruction is bona fide for a morph detector; under the second it is not a valid bona fide, and under ICAO and national rules it is not an admissible portrait. Still missing: any study that measures false alarms of morph detectors on one-photo GAN or diffusion reconstructions or AI-restored photos; the only measured analogue is the smoothing-filter preprint of Concas et al. (weak: two CNNs, BPCER values all multiples of 10), plus print-scan false detections reported by NIST and Ferrara et al.

Smaller corrections. Concas et al. has a stated venue (IEEE MetroXRAINE 2025) and a different author order. 'CVPRW 2024' for arXiv:2501.09817 is not verified. Tapia et al. raise the beautification question in the abstract and frame it as morph evasion. The ISO/IEC 20059, 39794-5 and 30107 definitions remain unverified and must be read before any claim about standards is final.
